channel.description: Tutorials in R with the code on every page: psychometrics, adaptive testing, scale validation, statistics, machine learning and data visualisation with real data.

item.title: Weighted Least Squares: How Closely Do Schools’ Reading and Writing Scores Go Together?
item.description: Weighted least squares (WLS) in R with lm(weights = ), on the 2012 SAT results of about 420 New York City high schools: heteroscedasticity, the Breusch–Pagan test, known weights (each row is a mean of n students), estimated weights (feasible WLS), robust sandwich standard errors as the alternative, variance weights against frequency and survey weights, residual checks after weighting and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Weighted least squares (WLS) in R with lm(weights = ), on the 2012 SAT results of about 420 New York City high schools: heteroscedasticity, the Breusch–Pagan test, known weights (each row is a mean of n students), estimated weights (feasible WLS), robust sandwich standard errors as the alternative, variance weights against frequency and survey weights, residual checks after weighting and APA reporting.

The question: can we trust every school’s average equally?

Every year, many students in New York City sit the SAT, the US college-entrance test. It has three sections: reading, mathematics and writing. The city publishes, for each high school, the average score of its students in each section, and the number of students who sat the test.

This page asks: how closely do a school’s average reading score and its average writing score go together? A regression of the writing average on the reading average gives a slope and a line.

There is a catch. The schools are very different in size. One school averages the scores of 6 students, another the scores of 1,277. An average of 6 students is far less reliable than an average of 1,277: it jumps around more from one year to the next. So the points on the chart are not equally precise, and ordinary regression treats them as if they were. This is called heteroscedasticity: the spread of the errors is not the same for every row.

Weighted least squares (WLS) fixes this by giving the precise rows more say than the imprecise ones. It is a special case of generalized least squares (see EXAMPLE_GENERALIZED_LEAST_SQUARES.Rmd), where the errors have unequal variances but no correlation between them. Ordinary multiple regression is explained in the hierarchical regression example; here we only look at what changes.

Code 
library(ggplot2)
library(lmtest)     # bptest(): Breusch–Pagan test; coeftest(): tests with a chosen covariance matrix
library(sandwich)   # vcovHC(): heteroscedasticity-consistent ("sandwich") covariance matrices
# one colour per model, the same in every chart
model_colours <- c("OLS" = "#2a78d6", "WLS, weights = n" = "#eb6834", "WLS, estimated weights" = "#1baf7a")
# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))

1. The data

NYC Open Data, the city’s open-data portal, publishes the 2012 SAT Results: one row per high school, free and with no login. We read it straight from the portal’s CSV address.

Code 
t0  <- Sys.time()
url <- "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/f9bf-2cp4.csv?$limit=1000"
raw <- read.csv(url)
seconds <- as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "secs"))
str(raw)
'data.frame':   478 obs. of  6 variables:
 $ dbn                           : chr  "01M292" "01M448" "01M450" "01M458" ...
 $ school_name                   : chr  "HENRY STREET SCHOOL FOR INTERNATIONAL STUDIES" "UNIVERSITY NEIGHBORHOOD HIGH SCHOOL" "EAST SIDE COMMUNITY SCHOOL" "FORSYTH SATELLITE ACADEMY" ...
 $ num_of_sat_test_takers        : chr  "29" "91" "70" "7" ...
 $ sat_critical_reading_avg_score: chr  "355" "383" "377" "414" ...
 $ sat_math_avg_score            : chr  "404" "423" "402" "401" ...
 $ sat_writing_avg_score         : chr  "363" "366" "370" "359" ...

The columns are the school code (dbn) and name, the number of students who took the SAT, and the average score in reading, mathematics and writing. The portal’s description says only “mean SAT scores” for the seniors of 2012 and gives no unit; the scores in the file run from 279 to 735, which fits the usual SAT scale of 200 to 800 points per section, but the file does not state it. The download took 6.3 seconds.

Some schools have the letter s instead of numbers. The file does not say why; it is most likely a rule that hides the results of very small groups. We cannot use these rows, so we drop them:

Code 
sat <- data.frame(school = raw$school_name,
                  n      = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(raw$num_of_sat_test_takers)),
                  read   = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(raw$sat_critical_reading_avg_score)),
                  math   = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(raw$sat_math_avg_score)),
                  write  = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(raw$sat_writing_avg_score)))
n_hidden <- sum(!complete.cases(sat))
sat <- sat[complete.cases(sat), ]
nrow(sat)
[1] 421
Code 
summary(sat[, c("n", "read", "write")])
       n               read           write    
 Min.   :   6.0   Min.   :279.0   Min.   :286  
 1st Qu.:  41.0   1st Qu.:368.0   1st Qu.:360  
 Median :  62.0   Median :391.0   Median :381  
 Mean   : 110.3   Mean   :400.9   Mean   :394  
 3rd Qu.:  95.0   3rd Qu.:416.0   3rd Qu.:411  
 Max.   :1277.0   Max.   :679.0   Max.   :682

That leaves 421 schools, after dropping 57 with hidden results. The smallest school in the file has 6 test takers, the largest 1,277, and half of the schools have fewer than 62. In all, the schools stand for 46,445 students. Each row is a mean, and the means rest on very different numbers of students.

2. Look at the data

Code 
ols <- lm(write ~ read, data = sat)
ggplot(sat, aes(read, write)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), alpha = 0.45, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#eb6834", linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 6, breaks = c(50, 250, 1000), name = "test takers") +
  labs(title = "Writing against reading: school averages",
       x = "average reading score", y = "average writing score") +
  theme_bw()

The schools lie close to a straight line. The size of each point is the number of students. The big points hug the line, and the small ones scatter more around it. The residuals show it more clearly:

Code 
sat$fitted <- fitted(ols)
sat$resid  <- resid(ols)
ggplot(sat, aes(n, resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10, 30, 100, 300, 1000)) +
  labs(title = "OLS residuals fan out in the small schools",
       x = "test takers (log scale)", y = "residual (points)") +
  theme_bw()

A funnel: wide on the left, where the schools are small, and narrow on the right. The usual first check is a plot of the residuals against the fitted values, and it is worth doing. But here the fitted values do not drive the spread: the number of students does, so the plot against n shows it best. In general, plot the residuals against the fitted values, against each predictor and against anything that could change the precision of a row.

Code 
bands <- cut(sat$n, c(0, 25, 50, 100, 200, Inf),
             labels = c("under 25", "25–50", "51–100", "101–200", "over 200"))
spread <- tapply(sat$resid, bands, sd)

The standard deviation of the residuals falls from 22.5 points in the schools with fewer than 25 test takers to 9.1 points in the schools with more than 200.

3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: ordinary least squares

\[\text{write}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \,\text{read}_i + \varepsilon_i\]

Ordinary least squares (OLS) finds the \(\beta\)’s that minimise the sum of squared residuals, \(\sum_i e_i^2\). Every row counts the same. It assumes homoscedasticity: all errors have the same variance, \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2\).

Step 2: what goes wrong when the variances differ

Suppose instead that \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma_i^2\) differs from row to row. Then OLS is affected in two ways:

  • The estimates stay unbiased. On average, over many samples, \(\hat\beta\) is still \(\beta\), as long as the mean model is right.
  • The standard errors are wrong. The usual formula, \(\hat\sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}\), assumes one common \(\sigma^2\). With unequal variances, the t tests, p values and confidence intervals can be too narrow or too wide, and there is no way to tell which from the output.
  • OLS is no longer the best. It is not the linear unbiased estimator with the smallest variance (the Gauss–Markov theorem needs equal variances). There is a more precise one, WLS.

Step 3: weighted least squares

WLS minimises a weighted sum of squares:

\[\sum_i w_i\, e_i^2 \qquad \text{with} \qquad w_i = \frac{1}{\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i)}\]

A row with a large variance has a small weight, so it pulls the line less. In matrix form, with \(W\) a diagonal matrix of the weights:

\[\hat\beta_{WLS} = (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top W y\]

Only the ratios of the weights matter. Multiplying all weights by 10 changes nothing in the estimates, and the standard errors are rescaled by the residual standard error. The weights are not parameters to estimate in the usual way: they must come from somewhere. There are two cases.

Step 4a: known weights, when each row is a mean

If row \(i\) is the mean of \(n_i\) people, and the people vary around the line with variance \(\sigma^2\), then the mean has variance

\[\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n_i} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad w_i = n_i\]

The weight is the number of people. This is the textbook case of known weights, and in R it is lm(y ~ x, weights = n).

It assumes that the variance comes only from averaging people. If schools also differ from each other for other reasons, for example in how well they teach, that adds a constant \(\tau^2\) that does not shrink with \(n_i\):

\[\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \tau^2 + \frac{\sigma^2}{n_i}\]

Then giving a school of 1,000 students 1,000 times the weight of a school of one student is too much. We will see which of the two holds in these data.

Step 4b: estimated weights (feasible WLS)

Often the variances are not known, and we must model them from the residuals:

  1. Fit OLS and keep the residuals \(e_i\).
  2. Model the variance: regress \(e_i^2\) (or \(\log e_i^2\)) on the variables that could change it. Here, on \(1/n_i\).
  3. Turn the fitted variances into weights, \(w_i = 1 / \widehat{\text{Var}}_i\).
  4. Refit by WLS.

This is feasible WLS (or feasible generalized least squares). It is not exact, because the weights are themselves estimates, and the standard errors from lm() do not take that uncertainty into account. With a few hundred rows and a simple variance model, this matters little.

Step 5: the other way out, keep OLS and fix the standard errors

OLS is still unbiased. So an alternative is to keep the OLS estimates and replace only the wrong standard errors with heteroscedasticity-consistent ones, also called robust or sandwich standard errors. The covariance matrix of \(\hat\beta\) is built as a sandwich:

\[\widehat{\text{Var}}(\hat\beta) = (X^\top X)^{-1} \Big( \sum_i e_i^2\, x_i x_i^\top \Big) (X^\top X)^{-1}\]

The squared residual \(e_i^2\) stands in for the unknown variance of each row, so no model for the variance is needed (White, 1980). The version called HC3 (MacKinnon & White, 1985; type = "HC3" in vcovHC()) is the safest for samples of this size (Long & Ervin, 2000).

WLS OLS with sandwich standard errors
Estimates Change (they are weighted) The same as OLS
Needs A good model for the variances Nothing about the variances
Efficiency Better, if the variance model is right Not improved: OLS stays inefficient
If the variance model is wrong Estimates still unbiased, but the usual standard errors are wrong (use sandwich with WLS too) Not applicable
Makes sense when The weights are known or well understood, as with group means The variance pattern is unknown, or you care only about valid inference

4. Fitting the model and reading the output

Is there heteroscedasticity? The Breusch–Pagan test

The Breusch–Pagan test (Breusch & Pagan, 1979) regresses the squared residuals on a set of variables. The null hypothesis is homoscedasticity. bptest() from lmtest uses the Koenker version, which does not need normal errors. By default it uses the predictors of the model, here the reading score:

Code 
bp_read <- bptest(ols)
bp_read

    studentized Breusch-Pagan test
data:  ols
BP = 0.898, df = 1, p-value = 0.3433

With the reading score as the only suspect, the test does not find a problem, \(\chi^2\)(1) = 0.90, p = .343. But the test only looks for variance that is linked to the variables we give it. The funnel is linked to the number of students, so we give it 1/n, the variable that the formula of step 4a points to:

Code 
bp_n <- bptest(ols, ~ I(1/n), data = sat)
bp_n

    studentized Breusch-Pagan test
data:  ols
BP = 102.3, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16

Now it is clear, \(\chi^2\)(1) = 102.3, p < .001. A non-significant test does not prove homoscedasticity: it means that this pattern was not found. Always look at the plots, and choose the variables for the test by thinking about where the variance comes from.

The OLS fit

Code 
summary(ols)

Call:
lm(formula = write ~ read, data = sat)
Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-63.292  -7.206   0.851   8.866  44.999 
Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -7.52321    4.93528  -1.524    0.128    
read         1.00164    0.01219  82.166   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
Residual standard error: 14.19 on 419 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9416,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9414 
F-statistic:  6751 on 1 and 419 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

The slope is 1.002 points of writing for each point of reading, with a standard error of 0.012. The slope is close to 1: a school with 10 points more in reading has about 10 points more in writing. \(R^2\) = .942, which is very high, as expected for averages of the same students.

WLS with known weights: weights = n

lm() takes the weights in its weights argument:

Code 
wls_n <- lm(write ~ read, data = sat, weights = n)
summary(wls_n)

Call:
lm(formula = write ~ read, data = sat, weights = n)
Weighted Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-369.59  -75.02   -7.79   60.09  420.08 
Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -24.036681   2.891675  -8.312 1.32e-15 ***
read          1.046313   0.006557 159.563  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
Residual standard error: 106 on 419 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9838,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9838 
F-statistic: 2.546e+04 on 1 and 419 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

The slope is now 1.046 and the intercept -24.0, against -7.5 with OLS. In the output, “Weighted Residuals” are \(\sqrt{w_i}\,e_i\), and the residual standard error is in those units, which is why it is 106.0 and not comparable to OLS’s 14.2 points. It is the estimate of \(\sigma\), the standard deviation of one student, under this model.

Do the weights \(w = n\) do their job? After weighting, the residuals \(\sqrt{n_i}\,e_i\) should have the same spread for all schools. We check this in section 6, but we can already see a warning in the variance model of the next step.

WLS with estimated weights

We follow the four steps of section 3. We regress the squared OLS residuals on \(1/n\):

\[e_i^2 = \tau^2 + \sigma^2 \,\frac{1}{n_i} + \text{error}\]

Code 
variance_model <- lm(resid^2 ~ I(1/n), data = sat)
tau2   <- coef(variance_model)[[1]]
sigma2 <- coef(variance_model)[[2]]
c(tau2 = tau2, sigma2 = sigma2)
      tau2     sigma2 
  29.48956 7121.57004

The intercept is \(\hat\tau^2\) = 29.5, a standard deviation of 5.4 points that every school has whatever its size. The slope is \(\hat\sigma^2\) = 7,122, a standard deviation of 84.4 points for one student. So a school of 10 students has a standard error of about 27.2 points, and a school of 1,000, 6.1: the floor \(\tau\) dominates for the big ones. This picture shows it, with the pure \(\sigma^2/n\) curve of known weights for comparison:

Code 
sigma2_only <- sum(sat$resid^2 / sat$n) / sum(1 / sat$n^2)   # least squares for e^2 = sigma^2 / n, no floor
grid <- data.frame(n = exp(seq(log(min(sat$n)), log(max(sat$n)), length.out = 200)))
curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(n = grid$n, sd = sqrt(tau2 + sigma2 / grid$n),  model = "floor + σ²/n"),
  data.frame(n = grid$n, sd = sqrt(sigma2_only / grid$n),    model = "σ²/n only (weights = n)"))
ggplot(sat, aes(n)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = abs(resid)), alpha = 0.35, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(y = sd, colour = model), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("floor + σ²/n" = "#1baf7a", "σ²/n only (weights = n)" = "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10, 30, 100, 300, 1000)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 70)) +
  labs(title = "How the typical error shrinks with school size",
       subtitle = "Points: absolute OLS residuals. Lines: the standard deviation each model expects",
       x = "test takers (log scale)", y = "points") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

The pure \(\sigma^2/n\) curve keeps falling, and goes under the points for the biggest schools. The curve with a floor flattens, as the data do. Now we turn the fitted variances into weights and refit:

Code 
sat$w <- 1 / fitted(variance_model)
wls_est <- lm(write ~ read, data = sat, weights = w)
summary(wls_est)

Call:
lm(formula = write ~ read, data = sat, weights = w)
Weighted Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-2.9155 -0.7596 -0.0614  0.5882  4.2261 
Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -18.82137    3.47691  -5.413 1.04e-07 ***
read          1.03322    0.00822 125.697  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
Residual standard error: 1.033 on 419 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9742,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9741 
F-statistic: 1.58e+04 on 1 and 419 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

The fitted variances are all positive here (35.1 to 1,216.4), which is not guaranteed for a regression of \(e^2\). If some were negative, or near zero, the weights would be nonsense. A safer way is to model the logarithm of the squared residuals, which can never give a negative variance:

Code 
log_model <- lm(log(resid^2) ~ log(n), data = sat)
wls_log   <- lm(write ~ read, data = sat, weights = 1 / exp(fitted(log_model)))
c(log_n_slope = unname(coef(log_model)[2]))
log_n_slope 
 -0.4573301

The variance goes with \(n^{-0.46}\): a pure \(\sigma^2/n\) would give \(-1\), and no dependence on the number of students would give 0. The data lie in between, as the floor suggested. The log version gives a slope of 1.028, almost the same as 1.033 from the first one. The two ways of modelling the variance agree. (One could also repeat the cycle, fitting again to the new residuals until nothing changes. One round is usually enough.)

The three lines

Code 
line_data <- data.frame(read = seq(min(sat$read), max(sat$read), length.out = 100))
lines_all <- rbind(
  data.frame(read = line_data$read, write = predict(ols,     line_data), model = "OLS"),
  data.frame(read = line_data$read, write = predict(wls_n,   line_data), model = "WLS, weights = n"),
  data.frame(read = line_data$read, write = predict(wls_est, line_data), model = "WLS, estimated weights"))
lines_all$model <- factor(lines_all$model, levels = names(model_colours))
ggplot(sat, aes(read, write)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey70", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = lines_all, aes(colour = model), linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_colours, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Three fitted lines through the same schools",
       x = "average reading score", y = "average writing score") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

The lines are close in the middle and part ways at the ends.

5. OLS against WLS, and the sandwich alternative

We put the estimates and the standard errors of the three fits side by side. For each fit, the standard errors are given in two ways: the usual ones from lm(), and the sandwich ones (HC3):

Code 
fits <- list("OLS" = ols, "WLS, weights = n" = wls_n, "WLS, estimated weights" = wls_est)
compare <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(m) {
  fit <- fits[[m]]
  usual  <- coef(summary(fit))
  robust <- coeftest(fit, vcov = vcovHC(fit, type = "HC3"))
  data.frame(model = m, term = rownames(usual),
             estimate = usual[, "Estimate"],
             se_usual = usual[, "Std. Error"],
             se_hc3   = robust[, "Std. Error"],
             row.names = NULL)
}))
compare[, 3:5] <- round(compare[, 3:5], 3)
compare
                   model        term estimate se_usual se_hc3
1                    OLS (Intercept)   -7.523    4.935  5.553
2                    OLS        read    1.002    0.012  0.014
3       WLS, weights = n (Intercept)  -24.037    2.892  4.704
4       WLS, weights = n        read    1.046    0.007  0.011
5 WLS, estimated weights (Intercept)  -18.821    3.477  4.538
6 WLS, estimated weights        read    1.033    0.008  0.011
Code 
get <- function(m, term, col) compare[compare$model == m & compare$term == term, col]
ratio_ols <- get("OLS", "read", "se_hc3") / get("OLS", "read", "se_usual")

What the table says:

  • The OLS standard errors were wrong. With sandwich errors, the standard error of the OLS slope is 0.014 instead of 0.012, 1.17 times as large. The usual output was too optimistic here, and the confidence interval is wider than the one lm() printed. The slope is still very significant, so the conclusion is the same, but with another dataset it might not be. The direction of the error is not fixed: in the simulation below the usual standard error is, on the contrary, too large.
  • The estimates move. The slope is 1.002 with OLS, 1.046 with weights \(n\) and 1.033 with estimated weights. The intercept goes from -7.5 to -24.0 and -18.8. If the model were exactly right, all three would estimate the same thing and differ only by chance. The intercept of the estimated-weights fit is 11.3 points away from the OLS one, which is 2.0 times the sandwich standard error of the OLS intercept. This is not a formal test, but it hints that the straight line fits the small schools and the big schools a little differently. The file cannot tell us why, and the large schools may differ from the small ones in more than size. Weighting changes which schools the line follows, so the two answers are answers to slightly different questions (Solon et al., 2015).
  • WLS is more precise, when compared fairly. Compare the sandwich errors, which are valid for every fit: the slope has 0.014 for OLS, 0.011 with weights \(n\) and 0.011 with estimated weights. That is the gain that the weights are meant to bring. The simulation below shows a clearer gain, when the variance model is exactly right.
  • The usual WLS errors are too small here. For WLS with \(w = n\) the usual and the sandwich errors differ (0.007 against 0.011), which says that the weights \(n\) do not describe the variance well. With the estimated weights the gap is smaller but still there (0.008 against 0.011): even this variance model is not perfect, and the variance may depend on more than the number of students. When in doubt, use WLS and sandwich errors: the weights buy precision, and the sandwich protects against a wrong variance model.

Proof by simulation: unbiased, but with wrong errors

To see the claims of step 2 at work, we generate 2,000 new data sets that follow the variance model we found, with a known slope, and fit both models to each:

Code 
set.seed(2025)
reps   <- 2000
true_b <- c(0, 1)
X      <- cbind(1, sat$read)
sd_i   <- sqrt(tau2 + sigma2 / sat$n)              # the standard deviation of each school
wt     <- 1 / sd_i^2                               # the ideal weights: 1 / variance
XtX_inv   <- solve(crossprod(X))
XtWX_inv  <- solve(crossprod(X, X * wt))
sim <- t(replicate(reps, {
  y   <- drop(X %*% true_b) + rnorm(nrow(X), 0, sd_i)
  b_o <- XtX_inv %*% crossprod(X, y)
  e_o <- y - X %*% b_o
  b_w <- XtWX_inv %*% crossprod(X, wt * y)
  c(ols = b_o[2], wls = b_w[2],
    se_ols_usual = sqrt(sum(e_o^2) / (nrow(X) - 2) * XtX_inv[2, 2]))
}))
colMeans(sim)
         ols          wls se_ols_usual 
  0.99964236   0.99989103   0.01213058
Code 
apply(sim, 2, sd)
         ols          wls se_ols_usual 
0.0101162999 0.0080339089 0.0005981061

The true slope is 1.

  • Unbiased: the average OLS slope is 1.000 and the average WLS slope 1.000. Both hit the target.
  • Inefficient: the slope of OLS varies from sample to sample with a standard deviation of 0.010, that of WLS with 0.008. WLS is 1.26 times as precise.
  • Wrong standard errors: the OLS standard error that lm() prints averages 0.012, while the true spread is 0.010.
Code 
sim_long <- data.frame(slope = c(sim[, "ols"], sim[, "wls"]),
                       model = rep(c("OLS", "WLS"), each = reps))
ggplot(sim_long, aes(slope, colour = model, fill = model)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("OLS" = "#2a78d6", "WLS" = "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("OLS" = "#2a78d6", "WLS" = "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "2,000 simulated slopes, OLS and WLS",
       subtitle = "Both centre on the true slope (dashed line); WLS is narrower",
       x = "estimated slope", y = "density") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

6. Checking the model after weighting

After weighting, what should be flat is not the raw residual but the weighted (or standardised) one. For a fit with weights, \(\sqrt{w_i}\,e_i\) should have the same spread for all rows. rstandard() divides further by the estimated \(\sigma\) and by a leverage term, and understands weights.

Code 
check <- rbind(
  data.frame(n = sat$n, fitted = fitted(ols),     r = rstandard(ols),     model = "OLS"),
  data.frame(n = sat$n, fitted = fitted(wls_n),   r = rstandard(wls_n),   model = "WLS, weights = n"),
  data.frame(n = sat$n, fitted = fitted(wls_est), r = rstandard(wls_est), model = "WLS, estimated weights"))
check$model <- factor(check$model, levels = names(model_colours))
ggplot(check, aes(n, r, colour = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10, 100, 1000)) +
  labs(title = "Standardised residuals against school size",
       x = "test takers (log scale)", y = "standardised residual") +
  theme_bw()

Left, OLS still has the funnel. In the middle, the weights \(n\) turn it round: now the big schools scatter more than the small ones, an overcorrection, which is what the floor \(\tau^2\) explained. Right, the estimated weights give a much more even band. A table shows the same by size of school:

Code 
sd_by_band <- sapply(list("OLS" = ols, "WLS, weights = n" = wls_n, "WLS, estimated weights" = wls_est),
                     function(m) tapply(rstandard(m), bands, sd))
knitr::kable(round(sd_by_band, 2), format = "pipe")
OLS WLS, weights = n WLS, estimated weights
under 25 1.59 0.72 0.84
25–50 0.94 0.82 0.92
51–100 0.83 0.97 1.02
101–200 0.72 1.06 1.04
over 200 0.65 1.46 1.10

The standard deviation of the standardised residuals should be near 1 in every row. For OLS it falls from 1.59 to 0.65, with weights \(n\) it rises from 0.72 to 1.46, and with estimated weights it stays between 0.84 and 1.10.

Other checks work as for any regression:

  • Linearity: plot the standardised residuals against the predictor, and check there is no curve (see EXAMPLE_POLYNOMIAL_REGRESSION.Rmd).
  • Outliers and influence: a few schools have large standardised residuals. cooks.distance() and hatvalues() work with weights too. If outliers are the main worry, see EXAMPLE_ROBUST_REGRESSION.Rmd.
  • Normality: it matters little with 421 rows, thanks to the central limit theorem.
  • Run the Breusch–Pagan test again, on the standardised residuals. The same test that found the problem should now find less of it. The test is simple enough to do by hand (Koenker’s version): regress the squared standardised residuals on \(1/n\), and take the number of rows times \(R^2\), which follows a \(\chi^2\) distribution with 1 degree of freedom. We do it by hand because bptest() on a weighted fit gave, for the weights \(n\), a statistic larger than the number of rows, which this version of the test cannot produce, so we do not rely on it here.
Code 
bp_by_hand <- function(fit) {
  aux  <- lm(rstandard(fit)^2 ~ I(1/sat$n))
  stat <- nobs(aux) * summary(aux)$r.squared
  c(statistic = stat, p = pchisq(stat, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
}
bp_after <- rbind("OLS" = bp_by_hand(ols), "WLS, weights = n" = bp_by_hand(wls_n),
                  "WLS, estimated weights" = bp_by_hand(wls_est))
round(bp_after, 3)
                       statistic     p
OLS                      101.831 0.000
WLS, weights = n           5.869 0.015
WLS, estimated weights     0.265 0.607

Against \(1/n\), the statistic is 101.8 for OLS (p < .001), 5.9 with weights \(n\) (p = .015) and 0.3 with the estimated weights (p = .607). The by-hand version for OLS matches bptest()’s 102.3, as it should.

7. Things to keep in mind

Variance weights, frequency weights and survey weights are different things

Many programs have one box called “weights”, and people put in three different things. They give the same estimates, but different standard errors:

Kind What a weight of \(w_i\) means Use when Standard errors
Variance (precision) weights The row has variance \(\sigma^2 / w_i\) Rows are means of \(n_i\) people, or measurements of known precision This page: lm(weights = )
Frequency weights The row stands for \(w_i\) identical cases A table of counts instead of a long data set The sample size is \(\sum w_i\), not the number of rows
Survey (sampling) weights The row stands for \(w_i\) people in the population, because it was sampled with probability \(1/w_i\) A complex survey, to estimate for the population Need the survey design: survey::svyglm()

lm(weights = ) always treats the weights as variance weights. Here is what happens if you wrongly think of the \(n\) as a frequency, that is, if you take each school to be \(n_i\) separate identical students:

Code 
df_rows <- df.residual(wls_n)               # the number of schools, minus 2
df_freq <- sum(sat$n) - 2                   # the number of students, minus 2
se_variance  <- summary(wls_n)$coefficients["read", 2]
se_frequency <- se_variance * sqrt(df_rows / df_freq)

The slope would have a standard error of 0.0006 instead of 0.0066, which is 10.5 times too small. The schools are 421 pieces of information, not 46,445. A frequency weight multiplies the information, a variance weight only redistributes it. If your weights are survey weights, do not use lm(weights = ) for inference at all: the errors need the design of the survey, or at least sandwich errors, and the survey weights are there to make the estimate represent the population, not to make it more precise.

Weighting changes the question

OLS answers “what is the line through the schools?”, WLS answers “what is the line, in which the schools with more information count more?”. If the straight line is exactly right, the two agree and the weights only add precision. If the two lines differ a lot, as with the intercepts of section 5, the model is probably wrong somewhere, and the weights should not hide it. Find the reason, rather than choose the line you prefer.

The caveats of these data

  • Averages of averages. These are school means, not students. A line through schools says how the school averages go together, which may not be how a student’s writing goes with their reading (the ecological fallacy).
  • The same students sit all three sections, so the high correlation between reading and writing is partly built in.
  • Only students who took the SAT, and in 2012 only. The schools with hidden results are not in the data.
  • The file does not state the scale of the scores or why some are hidden, as noted in section 1.

Other warnings

  • Wrong weights can mislead. If the weights follow a wrong idea of the variance, for example the pure \(\sigma^2 / n\) here, the standard errors of the usual output are wrong again. Use sandwich errors for safety.
  • Estimated weights come with uncertainty that lm() ignores. For large samples it does not matter. For small ones, bootstrap the whole procedure, or use nlme::gls() with a varFunc (for example varPower()), which estimates the variance function and the coefficients together by maximum likelihood (see EXAMPLE_GENERALIZED_LEAST_SQUARES.Rmd).
  • Heteroscedasticity can be the finding. If the spread itself is what interests you, for example if the best students vary more than the weak ones, model it, or use quantile regression, which describes the whole distribution of the outcome rather than one line through its middle.
  • Transforming the outcome (for example, taking logs) is another remedy when the spread grows with the mean, at the price of changing the meaning of the coefficients.

8. Reporting the results in APA style

A report (APA 7th edition) needs the data and the unit of analysis, the test that showed the heteroscedasticity, where the weights came from, the estimates with their uncertainty, and what the robust standard errors say. The numbers come from the R objects:

Code 
ci_est  <- confint(wls_est)
rob_est <- coeftest(wls_est, vcov = vcovHC(wls_est, type = "HC3"))
ci_rob  <- coefci(wls_est, vcov. = vcovHC(wls_est, type = "HC3"))
r2_est  <- summary(wls_est)$r.squared
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Model        = c("OLS", "OLS", "WLS, weights = n", "WLS, weights = n", "WLS, estimated weights", "WLS, estimated weights"),
  Term         = rep(c("Intercept", "Reading"), 3),
  `*b*`        = f3(compare$estimate),
  `SE`         = f3(compare$se_usual),
  `SE (HC3)`   = f3(compare$se_hc3),
  check.names = FALSE)

Method (data analysis):

We analysed the 2012 SAT results of 421 New York City high schools (NYC Department of Education, 2013), after removing 57 schools whose results were not published. Each row is a school mean based on between 6 and 1,277 students (M = 110.3, Mdn = 62). We regressed the mean writing score on the mean reading score. Because school means rest on very different numbers of students, we tested for heteroscedasticity with the studentised Breusch–Pagan test (Koenker, 1981), and we compared ordinary least squares (OLS) with weighted least squares (WLS), using weights equal to the number of test takers and weights estimated from a regression of the squared OLS residuals on the reciprocal of the number of test takers. We report heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC3) standard errors (MacKinnon & White, 1985). Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the packages lmtest (Zeileis & Hothorn, 2002) and sandwich (Zeileis, 2004).

Results:

The residuals of the OLS model were more spread out in schools with fewer test takers, Breusch–Pagan χ²(1) = 102.3, p < .001 (for the reciprocal of the number of test takers); the standard deviation of the residuals was 22.5 points in schools with fewer than 25 test takers and 9.1 points in schools with more than 200. In the model with estimated weights, each point of reading score went with 1.03 points of writing score, b = 1.033, 95% CI [1.017, 1.049], SE = 0.008, R² = .974. With HC3 standard errors, the 95% CI was [1.011, 1.055]. The OLS slope was 1.002 with a model-based standard error of 0.012, which rose to 0.014 with HC3 standard errors (Table 1). Weights equal to the number of test takers over-corrected: the standardised residuals then grew with school size, from SD = 0.72 to 1.46, because schools also differ by a variance that does not shrink with size, estimated here as SD = 5.4 points.

Table 1

Regression of Average Writing Score on Average Reading Score in 421 New York City High Schools

Model Term b SE SE (HC3)
OLS Intercept -7.523 4.935 5.553
OLS Reading 1.002 0.012 0.014
WLS, weights = n Intercept -24.037 2.892 4.704
WLS, weights = n Reading 1.046 0.007 0.011
WLS, estimated weights Intercept -18.821 3.477 4.538
WLS, estimated weights Reading 1.033 0.008 0.011

Note. b = unstandardised coefficient. SE = standard error from lm(); SE (HC3) = heteroscedasticity-consistent standard error. Estimated weights are the reciprocals of the fitted values of a regression of the squared OLS residuals on 1/n, where n is the number of test takers.

Points to remember:

  • Say what the rows are (here, school means) and how many people each one rests on.
  • Report the test for heteroscedasticity and the variable it was tested against.
  • Say where the weights came from, and which kind of weights they are (variance weights).
  • Give robust standard errors, or say why you did not need them.
  • Show that the weighting worked, with the standardised residuals.
  • If OLS and WLS disagree, say so and offer an explanation.

9. Summary

When The spread of the errors differs from row to row: means of groups of different size, measurements of known precision, or a spread that grows with a predictor
The problem OLS stays unbiased, but its standard errors are wrong and it is not the most precise estimator
Spotting it Residuals against fitted values, against each predictor and against the group size; lmtest::bptest(fit, ~ z, data = d) for the variable \(z\) you suspect
WLS Minimise \(\sum w_i e_i^2\), with \(w_i = 1 / \text{Var}(\varepsilon_i)\); in R, lm(y ~ x, weights = w)
Known weights A mean of \(n_i\) people has variance \(\sigma^2 / n_i\), so \(w_i = n_i\), unless there is also a variance that does not shrink with \(n_i\)
Estimated weights Regress \(e_i^2\) (or \(\log e_i^2\)) on the suspected variables, take \(w_i = 1 / \widehat{\text{Var}}_i\), refit
Alternative Keep OLS, and use sandwich standard errors: coeftest(fit, vcov = vcovHC(fit, type = "HC3"))
Do not confuse Variance weights (lm(weights = )) with frequency weights and survey weights
Checking The standardised residuals, rstandard(), against the variable that drives the variance
Related pages Generalized least squares, robust regression, quantile regression

References

Breusch, T. S., & Pagan, A. R. (1979). A simple test for heteroscedasticity and random coefficient variation. Econometrica, 47(5), 1287–1294. https://doi.org/10.2307/1911963

Koenker, R. (1981). A note on studentizing a test for heteroscedasticity. Journal of Econometrics, 17(1), 107–112. https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-4076(81)90062-2

Long, J. S., & Ervin, L. H. (2000). Using heteroscedasticity consistent standard errors in the linear regression model. The American Statistician, 54(3), 217–224. https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2000.10474549

MacKinnon, J. G., & White, H. (1985). Some heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance matrix estimators with improved finite sample properties. Journal of Econometrics, 29(3), 305–325. https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-4076(85)90158-7

NYC Department of Education. (2013). 2012 SAT results [Data set]. NYC Open Data. https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Education/2012-SAT-Results/f9bf-2cp4

Solon, G., Haider, S. J., & Wooldridge, J. M. (2015). What are we weighting for? Journal of Human Resources, 50(2), 301–316. https://doi.org/10.3368/jhr.50.2.301

White, H. (1980). A heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance matrix estimator and a direct test for heteroskedasticity. Econometrica, 48(4), 817–838. https://doi.org/10.2307/1912934

Zeileis, A. (2004). Econometric computing with HC and HAC covariance matrix estimators. Journal of Statistical Software, 11(10), 1–17. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v011.i10

Zeileis, A., & Hothorn, T. (2002). Diagnostic checking in regression relationships. R News, 2(3), 7–10.

This post first appeared on Worked Examples in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Robust Regression: When a Few Countries Pull the Line
item.description: Robust regression in R with MASS::rlm() and robustbase::lmrob(), on World Bank data for about 190 countries: life expectancy against health spending. Why least squares is fragile, outliers, leverage and influence, M-estimation with Huber and bisquare weights, MM-estimation and the breakdown point, what to do with outliers instead of deleting them, robust against sandwich standard errors, and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Robust regression in R with MASS::rlm() and robustbase::lmrob(), on World Bank data for about 190 countries: life expectancy against health spending. Why least squares is fragile, outliers, leverage and influence, M-estimation with Huber and bisquare weights, MM-estimation and the breakdown point, what to do with outliers instead of deleting them, robust against sandwich standard errors, and APA reporting.

The question: do a few odd countries decide the answer?

Countries that spend more on health have longer-living people. But how much longer, for each extra dollar? To answer, we draw a line through about 190 countries and read its slope.

Some countries do not follow the pattern. The Central African Republic spends little and its people live much shorter than even that low spending predicts. A few small island states spend a lot and do not live longer. Ordinary least squares (OLS) gives every country the same say, and lets such countries drag the line towards them.

This page asks: how much does one tenfold step in health spending buy in life expectancy, when we do not let a handful of odd countries decide? The answer is robust regression: estimation that resists outliers.

Resists outliers in \(y\) Resists bad leverage points Efficient when data are clean
OLS (lm()) no no the best
M-estimation (rlm()) yes no high (about 95%)
MM-estimation (lmrob()) yes yes high (about 95%)
LTS (lqs()) yes yes low

The columns are explained in section 3. This page does not re-teach ordinary regression: see hierarchical regression for that.

Code 
library(MASS)       # rlm() and lqs(): robust regression (comes with R)
library(robustbase) # lmrob(): MM-estimation (a CRAN package, not part of R)
library(sandwich)   # vcovHC(): heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors
library(lmtest)     # coeftest(), bptest()
library(jsonlite)   # fromJSON(): reads the World Bank API
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)    # labels that do not overlap
# one colour per method, the same in every chart
method_colours <- c("OLS" = "#2a78d6", "Huber" = "#eb6834", "Bisquare" = "#1baf7a",
                    "MM" = "#eda100", "LTS" = "#e87ba4")
# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
# the sensitivity analysis of section 5: alter the spending of k_bad of the n_poor lowest spenders
k_bad  <- 12
n_poor <- 30

1. The data

The World Bank publishes the World Development Indicators through an open API: free, no key and no login. We take two indicators for the year 2021 and the list of countries:

  • SH.XPD.CHEX.PC.CD: current health expenditure per capita, in current US dollars. The World Bank gets it from the WHO Global Health Expenditure Database. “Current” means money spent in that year on health goods and services (not on buildings); “per capita” means per person.
  • SP.DYN.LE00.IN: life expectancy at birth, in years: how long a newborn would live if the death rates of that year stayed the same for life. It comes from the United Nations World Population Prospects and national statistical offices.
  • The country list, with region and income group, which tells countries from aggregates such as “World” or “Sub-Saharan Africa”. The indicators contain both.
Code 
base <- "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/"
urls <- c(spend     = paste0(base, "country/all/indicator/SH.XPD.CHEX.PC.CD?format=json&date=2021&per_page=400"),
          life      = paste0(base, "country/all/indicator/SP.DYN.LE00.IN?format=json&date=2021&per_page=400"),
          countries = paste0(base, "country?format=json&per_page=400"))
started <- Sys.time()
files   <- sapply(urls, function(u) { f <- tempfile(fileext = ".json"); download.file(u, f, quiet = TRUE); f })
seconds <- as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), started, units = "secs"))
kilobytes <- sum(file.size(files)) / 1024
api <- lapply(files, fromJSON)
sapply(api, function(a) a[[1]]$pages)   # 1 each: everything arrived on the first page
    spend      life countries 
        1         1         1

The three downloads took 0.2 seconds and 235 kB together. Each answer has the number of pages in its first element and the records in its second, so [[2]] holds the data. We join the three, drop the aggregates and the countries with a missing value:

Code 
countries <- data.frame(iso3 = api$countries[[2]]$id, name = api$countries[[2]]$name,
                        region = api$countries[[2]]$region$value, income = api$countries[[2]]$incomeLevel$value)
health <- data.frame(iso3 = api$spend[[2]]$countryiso3code, spend = api$spend[[2]]$value)
life   <- data.frame(iso3 = api$life[[2]]$countryiso3code,  life  = api$life[[2]]$value)
d <- merge(merge(health, life, by = "iso3"), countries, by = "iso3")
n_all <- nrow(d)
d <- d[d$region != "Aggregates" & complete.cases(d), ]
d$logspend <- log10(d$spend)          # explained in section 2
rownames(d) <- d$name
n <- nrow(d)
head(d[order(d$spend), c("spend", "life", "region")], 4)
                      spend   life              region
Somalia, Fed. Rep. 15.01880 55.703 Sub-Saharan Africa 
Madagascar         17.17939 62.516 Sub-Saharan Africa 
Congo, Dem. Rep.   21.58849 60.044 Sub-Saharan Africa 
Sudan              21.69141 64.460 Sub-Saharan Africa

That leaves 192 countries and territories (the join had 261 rows, aggregates included). The terms of use: the World Bank licenses its own datasets under CC BY 4.0 by default (World Bank, n.d.), with attribution; the API does not say the licence of each single indicator, and the two used here come from the WHO and the United Nations, so check the terms of an indicator on its World Bank page before reusing it beyond a tutorial like this one. Names are as the World Bank writes them: “Naoero” is Nauru.

2. Look at the data

Code 
long <- rbind(data.frame(life = d$life, x = d$spend,        scale = "Spending in dollars"),
              data.frame(life = d$life, x = log10(d$spend), scale = "Log10 of spending"))
long$scale <- factor(long$scale, levels = c("Spending in dollars", "Log10 of spending"))
ggplot(long, aes(x, life)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey35", alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(v) num(v), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.1))) +
  labs(title = "Life expectancy against health spending, 2021",
       x = "health spending per person", y = "life expectancy (years)") +
  theme_bw()

The right panel shows the same points with the logarithm of spending on the axis. Look at the left panel first. Most countries crowd on the left, and a straight line through them would not describe the curve: the first dollars buy a lot of life, the ten-thousandth dollar very little. Taking the logarithm of spending, base 10, turns equal ratios into equal steps, and the cloud becomes straight. So we model

\[\text{life}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log_{10}(\text{spend}_i) + \varepsilon_i\]

and \(\beta_1\) is the gain in life expectancy for each tenfold increase in spending. Doubling is a smaller step: \(\beta_1 \times \log_{10} 2\).

Code 
ols <- lm(life ~ logspend, data = d)
ggplot(d, aes(spend, life)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey35", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(ols)[[1]], slope = coef(ols)[[2]], colour = method_colours[["OLS"]]) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = function(v) num(v), breaks = c(10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000)) +
  labs(title = "On a log scale the cloud is straight",
       x = "health spending per person (US$, log scale)", y = "life expectancy (years)") +
  theme_bw()

The OLS line is 47.9 + 8.84 \(\times \log_{10}\)(spend): each tenfold increase goes with 8.8 more years of life, and a doubling with 2.7. Some points lie far from the line, mostly below it.

3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: why least squares is fragile

OLS chooses the line that makes the sum of squared residuals \(\sum_i e_i^2\) as small as possible, where \(e_i = y_i - \hat y_i\). Squaring is the problem: a country that is 20 years off the line costs \(400\), a hundred times as much as one that is 2 years off. To save that cost, the line moves towards it. One bad point can move the OLS line as far as it likes. To see this, we take one country with a high spending, Switzerland, and slide its life expectancy from 0 to 120 years. At each value we refit the line:

Code 
slide <- seq(0, 120, by = 4)
slope_when <- function(value) {
  z <- d
  z["Switzerland", "life"] <- value
  c(OLS = coef(lm(life ~ logspend, z))[[2]],
    Huber = coef(rlm(life ~ logspend, z))[[2]],
    Bisquare = coef(rlm(life ~ logspend, z, psi = psi.bisquare))[[2]])
}
slides <- t(sapply(slide, slope_when))
slides <- data.frame(value = rep(slide, 3), slope = c(slides), method = rep(colnames(slides), each = length(slide)))
slides$method <- factor(slides$method, levels = c("OLS", "Huber", "Bisquare"))
swiss <- d["Switzerland", ]
range_by <- tapply(slides$slope, slides$method, function(s) diff(range(s)))
Code 
ggplot(slides, aes(value, slope, colour = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = swiss$life, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = swiss$life - 1.5, y = max(slides$slope), label = "actual value",
           hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 3.3, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = method_colours) +
  labs(title = "Moving one country's life expectancy",
       x = "life expectancy given to Switzerland (years)", y = "estimated slope (years per tenfold)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

The OLS slope follows the value we gave Switzerland in a straight line: it moves by 1.7 years per tenfold across the range, and nothing stops it. The robust slopes move by 0.2 (Huber) and 0.2 (bisquare): the further away the point is, the less it matters, and that is what we want to build.

Step 2: three kinds of unusual point

“Outlier” is used for three different things, with three different checks. All three come from the OLS fit, with \(p = 2\) parameters and \(n\) points:

Kind What it is Measure
Outlier in \(y\) far from the line, up or down, at a usual \(x\) studentized residual \(t_i\): the residual divided by its standard error, with the point left out of the fit. Beyond \(\pm 2\) or \(\pm 3\) is unusual
High-leverage point far from the other points in \(x\), wherever its \(y\) is hat value \(h_i\), the diagonal of \(H = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\). The average is \(p/n\); above \(2p/n\) is high
Influential point removing it changes the fit a lot Cook’s distance \(D_i = \dfrac{e_i^2}{p\,s^2}\dfrac{h_i}{(1 - h_i)^2}\): large when both the residual and the leverage are large. A common flag is \(4/n\)

A high-leverage point that sits on the trend is a good leverage point: it makes the line more precise. One that sits off the trend is a bad leverage point, and is the most dangerous kind: it has the leverage to pull the line, and the residual to pull it the wrong way. Because the line bends towards it, its own residual in OLS is small, and the point hides itself.

Step 3: M-estimation, the idea

Instead of squares, M-estimation (the “M” is for maximum likelihood type; Huber, 1964) minimises a loss function \(\rho\) of the scaled residuals:

\[\hat\beta = \arg\min_\beta \sum_{i=1}^{n} \rho\!\left(\frac{e_i}{s}\right), \qquad e_i = y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^\top\beta\]

\(s\) is a robust scale: an estimate of the typical size of a residual that outliers do not inflate, usually the median absolute residual divided by 0.6745 (so that it equals the standard deviation for normal errors). With \(\rho(u) = u^2/2\) this is OLS. Robust methods replace \(\rho\) by a function that grows more slowly. The derivative \(\psi = \rho'\) is the influence function: how hard a residual of size \(u\) pulls on the line. The weight is \(w(u) = \psi(u)/u\).

\(\rho(u)\) \(\psi(u)\) \(w(u)\)
Least squares \(u^2/2\) \(u\) \(1\)
Huber, \(k = 1.345\) \(u^2/2\) if \(\lvert u\rvert \le k\), else \(k\lvert u\rvert - k^2/2\) \(u\) if \(\lvert u\rvert \le k\), else \(k\,\mathrm{sign}(u)\) \(1\) if \(\lvert u\rvert \le k\), else \(k/\lvert u\rvert\)
Tukey’s bisquare, \(c = 4.685\) \(\dfrac{c^2}{6}\left[1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{u^2}{c^2}\right)^3\right]\) if \(\lvert u\rvert \le c\), else \(\dfrac{c^2}{6}\) \(u\left(1 - \dfrac{u^2}{c^2}\right)^2\) if \(\lvert u\rvert \le c\), else \(0\) \(\left(1 - \dfrac{u^2}{c^2}\right)^2\) if \(\lvert u\rvert \le c\), else \(0\)

The constants \(k = 1.345\) and \(c = 4.685\) are chosen so that, when the errors really are normal, the estimator is 95% as efficient as OLS: its standard errors are only about 2.5% larger. They are the defaults of rlm() and lmrob().

Code 
huber_rho <- function(u, k = 1.345) ifelse(abs(u) <= k, u^2 / 2, k * abs(u) - k^2 / 2)
huber_psi <- function(u, k = 1.345) pmax(-k, pmin(k, u))
huber_w   <- function(u, k = 1.345) ifelse(abs(u) <= k, 1, k / abs(u))
bisq_rho  <- function(u, c = 4.685) ifelse(abs(u) <= c, c^2 / 6 * (1 - (1 - (u / c)^2)^3), c^2 / 6)
bisq_psi  <- function(u, c = 4.685) ifelse(abs(u) <= c, u * (1 - (u / c)^2)^2, 0)
bisq_w    <- function(u, c = 4.685) ifelse(abs(u) <= c, (1 - (u / c)^2)^2, 0)
# the formulas above agree with the ones inside MASS
u <- seq(-8, 8, by = 0.1)
c(huber = max(abs(huber_w(u) - psi.huber(u))), bisquare = max(abs(bisq_w(u) - psi.bisquare(u))))
   huber bisquare 
       0        0

  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ fn, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Least squares" = method_colours[["OLS"]],
                                 Huber = method_colours[["Huber"]], Bisquare = method_colours[["Bisquare"]])) +
  labs(title = "Loss, influence and weight of a residual",
       x = "scaled residual u = e / s", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Read the three panels from top to bottom:

  • Loss. OLS (blue) squares the residual, so the loss climbs steeply. Huber’s loss turns into a straight line after \(k\): big residuals cost much less. The bisquare loss stops growing altogether after \(c\): beyond that, it does not matter how far away a point is.
  • Influence. OLS influence grows with the residual forever. Huber’s is bounded: no residual pulls harder than \(k\). Bisquare’s redescends: it rises, falls back, and is exactly zero beyond \(c\). Such a point has no say at all.
  • Weight. Every OLS residual has weight 1. Huber gives weight \(k/\lvert u\rvert\) beyond \(k\): smaller, but never zero. Bisquare gives zero weight to residuals beyond \(c = 4.685\) scaled units.

Step 4: how R finds the numbers, by iteratively reweighted least squares

No formula gives the minimum of \(\sum\rho(e_i/s)\) directly, but the weights turn it into a series of ordinary regressions (iteratively reweighted least squares, IRLS):

  1. Fit OLS and compute the residuals \(e_i\).
  2. Estimate the scale \(s\) from the residuals, and the scaled residuals \(u_i = e_i/s\).
  3. Give every point the weight \(w_i = w(u_i)\).
  4. Fit a weighted least squares line with those weights: minimise \(\sum w_i e_i^2\). (For weighted least squares, see the page on it.)
  5. Go back to step 2, until the coefficients stop changing.

A country that the line fits badly gets a small weight, so next time the line follows it less, its residual stays large and its weight small. The final weights show who was ignored. We will do the loop by hand in section 4.

Step 5: the limit of M-estimators, and the breakdown point

M-estimators bound the influence of a large residual, but do nothing about leverage: a point far out in \(x\) drags the line so that its own residual is small, and so it keeps a large weight. Worse, IRLS starts from OLS, which the bad point has already ruined.

The breakdown point measures this in plain words: the share of the data that can be replaced by anything, however absurd, before the estimate can be taken anywhere you like.

  • OLS: one point, so a breakdown point of \(1/n\), almost 0%.
  • Huber M-estimator: it resists bad \(y\) values but a bad \(x\) value can break it, so with leverage points it too has a breakdown point of about \(1/n\).
  • Estimators with the highest possible breakdown point, 50%: the least trimmed squares (LTS, Rousseeuw, 1984), which minimises the sum of the smallest half of the squared residuals, and S-estimators. They resist up to nearly half of the data being bad. They are far less efficient when the data are clean.
  • MM-estimators (Yohai, 1987) combine the two: an S-estimate gives a first fit and a robust scale \(s\) (that is the 50% breakdown part), then a bisquare M-step starting from it, tuned for 95% efficiency. This is why lmrob() is the usual first choice today (Maronna et al., 2019).

The same numbers by hand: IRLS in six lines

Code 
X <- model.matrix(~ logspend, d)
y <- d$life
b <- coef(ols)                                     # step 1: start from OLS
for (i in 1:50) {
  e  <- y - X %*% b
  s  <- median(abs(e)) / 0.6745                    # step 2: robust scale
  w  <- huber_w(e / s)                             # step 3: Huber weights
  b_new <- solve(t(X) %*% (c(w) * X), t(X) %*% (c(w) * y))   # step 4: weighted least squares
  if (max(abs(b_new - b)) < 1e-8) break
  b <- b_new
}
rbind(by_hand = c(b), rlm = coef(huber))
        (Intercept) logspend
by_hand    48.35372 8.808177
rlm        48.35368 8.808184

The comparison

Code 
slope_row <- function(method, est, se, scale) {
  data.frame(method = method, intercept = est[1], slope = est[2], se = se, scale = scale,
             lower = est[2] - qnorm(.975) * se, upper = est[2] + qnorm(.975) * se)
}
robust_fits <- function(z) {
  fits <- list(OLS      = lm(life ~ logspend, z),
               Huber    = rlm(life ~ logspend, z),
               Bisquare = rlm(life ~ logspend, z, psi = psi.bisquare),
               MM       = lmrob(life ~ logspend, z))
  rows <- lapply(names(fits), function(m) {
    f <- fits[[m]]
    sm <- summary(f)$coefficients
    sc <- if (m == "OLS") summary(f)$sigma else if (m == "MM") f$scale else f$s
    slope_row(m, sm[, 1], sm[2, 2], sc)
  })
  list(fits = fits, table = do.call(rbind, rows))
}

5. Where M-estimation is not enough: bad leverage points

The real data have outliers but no bad leverage points, so every method gives much the same line. To see what happens when there is one, we damage the data on purpose. Suppose a data-entry error made the spending of the 12 countries with the shortest-lived people, among the 30 lowest spenders, a thousand times too large (a unit slip: that is 3 steps of \(\log_{10}\)). Those are the countries that pull the OLS line flat:

Code 
make_bad <- function(k, shift = 3) {
  poorest <- d[order(d$spend), ][seq_len(min(n, max(n_poor, round(2.5 * k)))), ]   # the lowest spenders
  bad     <- rownames(poorest)[order(poorest$life)][seq_len(k)]   # the k with the lowest life expectancy
  z <- d
  z[bad, "logspend"] <- z[bad, "logspend"] + shift
  z$altered <- rownames(z) %in% bad
  z
}
