With no trees the residuals are wide, the spread of the strength itself. Each tree takes a bite out of them, until only the part no tree can explain is left. Over the 100 trees the training error keeps falling; the question is whether the test error does too. That is the question of the next sections.

4. The settings

A boosted model has a few settings (hyperparameters) that the data cannot tell us. Each one controls how fast the model learns and how complex it can become:

Setting (xgboost name) What it does Typical values Too low Too high
Number of trees (nrounds) How many correction rounds 100 to several thousand Underfits Overfits
Learning rate (eta) How much of each tree is added 0.01 to 0.3 Needs very many trees Jumpy; overfits sooner
Tree depth (max_depth) Levels per tree. Depth 1 is a stump (no interactions), depth 2 allows two-way interactions, and so on 2 to 8 Misses interactions Overfits; slow
Row sampling (subsample) Share of the samples used for each tree 0.5 to 1 More noise No randomness against overfitting
Column sampling (colsample_bytree) Share of the predictors used for each tree 0.5 to 1 Trees too weak Trees too alike
Minimum child weight (min_child_weight) Fewest samples a leaf may rest on (for squared error) 1 to 10 Leaves fitted to noise Underfits
Penalties (lambda, gamma) Shrink leaf values (lambda) and ask a split to pay for itself (gamma) 0 to 10 Underfits

The settings work together. A smaller learning rate needs more trees; deeper trees need fewer. A good rule: set the learning rate low enough to be smooth (0.05 to 0.1), and let cross-validation choose the number of trees.

Learning rate and number of trees

To compare settings without touching the test set, we use 5-fold cross-validation on the training data: the training samples are split into five parts; the model is fitted five times, each time to four parts, and the error is measured on the fifth. xgb.cv() does it, and gives the error after every tree. We give it the same folds each time, so that the settings are compared on the same data.

Code 
set.seed(1)
folds <- split(sample(nrow(train)), rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(train)))
# cross-validation for a set of settings: returns the error after every tree
cv_run <- function(nrounds, early = NULL, ...) {
  params <- list(objective = "reg:squarederror", nthread = 1, ...)
  xgb.cv(params = params, data = d_train, nrounds = nrounds, folds = folds,
         early_stopping_rounds = early, verbose = 0)
}

Three learning rates, with trees of depth 4:

Code 
rates <- c(0.5, 0.1, 0.02)
lr_log <- do.call(rbind, lapply(rates, function(e) {
  cv <- cv_run(1500, eta = e, max_depth = 4)
  data.frame(eta = factor(e, levels = rates), trees = cv$evaluation_log$iter,
             rmse = cv$evaluation_log$test_rmse_mean)
}))
lr_best <- aggregate(rmse ~ eta, lr_log, min)
ggplot(lr_log, aes(trees, rmse, colour = eta)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = colours[1:3]) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(3.5, 10)) +
  labs(x = "Number of trees (log scale)", y = "Cross-validated RMSE (MPa)", colour = "Learning rate") +
  theme_bw()

The highest rate (0.5) learns fastest: it is the best of the three for the first hundred trees or so, but it flattens at 4.98 MPa. The middle rate (0.1) needs a few hundred trees and gets lower, to 4.48 MPa. The smallest rate (0.02) is still improving after the 1,500 trees tried here (4.62 MPa) and would need many more. A small learning rate lets the model go further, but costs trees and time; a middle value is a good compromise.

Overfitting: training error against validation error

A model with enough trees can learn the training data by heart, noise included. The training error then keeps falling, while the error on new data stops improving, and may turn up. To see it, we use larger trees (depth 6), where it happens sooner, and watch both errors tree by tree. The cross-validation error is the error on the part left out, the validation error.

Code 
# early_stopping_rounds = 30: stop when the validation error has not improved for 30 trees
cv_depth6 <- cv_run(3000, early = 30, eta = 0.1, max_depth = 6)
log6 <- cv_depth6$evaluation_log
best_n6 <- cv_depth6$early_stop$best_iteration
curve <- rbind(data.frame(trees = log6$iter, rmse = log6$train_rmse_mean, data = "Training"),
               data.frame(trees = log6$iter, rmse = log6$test_rmse_mean,  data = "Validation (cross-validation)"))
ggplot(curve, aes(trees, rmse, colour = data)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_n6, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = best_n6, y = 7.5, label = paste(best_n6, "trees"),
           hjust = 1.1, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = colours[1:2]) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 8)) +
  labs(x = "Number of trees", y = "RMSE (MPa)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

The training error keeps falling, down to 0.90 MPa after 409 trees. The validation error stops improving at 379 trees (4.74 MPa), and does not improve after that. The gap between the two lines is the overfitting: the model is better at the samples it has seen than at new ones.

Early stopping uses this: stop adding trees when the validation error has not improved for a number of rounds (here 30), and keep the number of trees that was best. The number of trees is therefore not set by hand but found by cross-validation. This is the usual way to choose it.

A small tuning grid

We now look at the other settings together. Trying every combination is costly, so we use a small grid: three learning rates, three depths, two minimum child weights and two row sampling rates, 36 combinations. For each, the number of trees is chosen by early stopping, and the cross-validated RMSE at that number is recorded. The column sampling is fixed at 0.8.

Code 
grid <- expand.grid(eta = c(0.3, 0.1, 0.05), max_depth = c(2, 4, 6),
                    min_child_weight = c(1, 5), subsample = c(0.7, 1))
grid$trees <- NA; grid$rmse <- NA
for (i in seq_len(nrow(grid))) {
  cv <- cv_run(3000, early = 30, eta = grid$eta[i], max_depth = grid$max_depth[i],
               min_child_weight = grid$min_child_weight[i], subsample = grid$subsample[i],
               colsample_bytree = 0.8)
  grid$trees[i] <- cv$early_stop$best_iteration
  grid$rmse[i]  <- cv$early_stop$best_score
}
grid <- grid[order(grid$rmse), ]
best <- grid[1, ]
knitr::kable(head(grid, 8), digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, align = "rrrrrr",
             col.names = c("Learning rate", "Depth", "Min. child weight", "Row sampling", "Trees", "CV RMSE"))
Learning rate Depth Min. child weight Row sampling Trees CV RMSE

0.10 4 1 0.7 435 4.28
0.10 4 5 1.0 799 4.28
0.05 6 5 0.7 651 4.28
0.05 4 5 0.7 837 4.30
0.05 4 1 0.7 597 4.30
0.10 4 5 0.7 508 4.30
0.05 4 5 1.0 1418 4.31

The best combination is a learning rate of 0.1, depth 4, minimum child weight 1 and row sampling of 1, with 888 trees and a cross-validated RMSE of 4.22 MPa. Look at the other rows too: several settings give almost the same error. The grid is small and the cross-validation itself has noise, so do not read too much into the exact winner; what matters is the region: trees of depth 4, and a learning rate of 0.05 to 0.1. The best result by depth:

5. Fitting the final model

We fit the model to all the training data with the chosen settings and number of trees:

Code 
params <- list(objective = "reg:squarederror", nthread = 1, eta = best$eta,
               max_depth = best$max_depth, min_child_weight = best$min_child_weight,
               subsample = best$subsample, colsample_bytree = 0.8)
set.seed(3)    # the row and column sampling are random
fit <- xgb.train(params = params, data = d_train, nrounds = best$trees)
fit
##### xgb.Booster
call:
  xgb.train(params = params, data = d_train, nrounds = best$trees)
# of features: 8 
# of rounds:  888

6. Does it beat simpler models? The test set

We now use the test set, once. The competitors, all fitted to the same training data:

  • Linear regression with the eight predictors, no interactions or curves.
  • A single regression tree (CART), pruned by cross-validation.
  • A random forest (ranger) with its default settings (500 trees).
  • Gradient boosting, tuned as above.
Code 
linear <- lm(strength ~ ., train)
set.seed(4)
tree <- rpart(strength ~ ., train)
tree <- prune(tree, cp = tree$cptable[which.min(tree$cptable[, "xerror"]), "CP"])
forest <- ranger(strength ~ ., train, seed = 5, num.threads = 1)
predictions <- data.frame(
  `Linear regression` = predict(linear, test),
  `Single tree`       = predict(tree, test),
  `Random forest`     = predict(forest, test)$predictions,
  `Gradient boosting` = predict(fit, x_test),
  check.names = FALSE)
# the three measures: the error on the strength scale, and the share of variance explained
metrics <- function(y, p) c(RMSE = sqrt(mean((y - p)^2)), MAE = mean(abs(y - p)),
                            R2 = 1 - sum((y - p)^2) / sum((y - mean(y))^2))
results <- t(sapply(predictions, function(p) metrics(test$strength, p)))
knitr::kable(results, digits = 2, align = "rrr")
RMSE MAE R2
Linear regression 10.43 8.41 0.61
Single tree 9.60 7.45 0.67
Random forest 5.66 4.43 0.89
Gradient boosting 3.93 2.78 0.95

RMSE and MAE (mean absolute error) are in MPa: smaller is better. \(R^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}\) is the share of the variance of the test strengths that the model explains. Linear regression is a baseline: its test RMSE is 10.43 MPa. The single tree is 9.60. The random forest reaches 5.66, and gradient boosting 3.93 MPa (\(R^2\) = .95). Gradient boosting’s typical mistake is 2.8 MPa, against a standard deviation of 16.8 MPa in the test strengths.

Code 
po <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(predictions), function(m)
  data.frame(model = factor(m, levels = names(predictions)), observed = test$strength, predicted = predictions[[m]])))
ggplot(po, aes(predicted, observed)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(colour = colours[1], alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Predicted strength (MPa)", y = "Actual strength (MPa)") +
  theme_bw()

The closer the points to the diagonal, the better the model. The straight line misses the curve; the single tree can only make a few steps; the forest follows the diagonal better, and the boosted model stays closest to it.

Two cautions. First, the test set has only 206 samples, so each of these numbers has some noise; the gap between boosting and the forest (1.72 MPa) is large, but a gap of a few hundredths of a MPa would mean little. Second, the random forest was not tuned here and boosting was; a tuned forest would come closer. The honest summary is not “boosting always wins” but that ensembles of trees beat the simple models when the relationship is curved and has interactions, and that boosting, with some tuning, did best here.

7. Interpreting the model

A boosted model is a black box in the sense that no single number says what a variable does. Three tools open it, from the whole model down to one sample.

Which predictors matter? Gain against permutation

There are two common ways to rank the predictors.

  • Gain is built into xgboost: the total improvement in the loss from all the splits on a predictor, as a share of the total. It is computed on the training data and says what the model used.
  • Permutation importance shuffles one predictor in the test set, so that it carries no information, and measures how much the error increases. It says what the model needs on new data. We write it by hand; it is only a loop.
Code 
gain <- as.data.frame(xgb.importance(model = fit))
gain <- setNames(gain$Gain, gain$Feature)[predictors]
set.seed(6)
baseline <- sqrt(mean((test$strength - predict(fit, x_test))^2))
permutation <- sapply(predictors, function(v) mean(replicate(20, {
  shuffled <- x_test
  shuffled[, v] <- sample(shuffled[, v])
  sqrt(mean((test$strength - predict(fit, shuffled))^2)) - baseline
})))
importance <- rbind(data.frame(predictor = predictors, share = gain / sum(gain), method = "Gain"),
                    data.frame(predictor = predictors, share = permutation / sum(permutation), method = "Permutation"))
importance$predictor <- factor(nice[importance$predictor], levels = nice[names(sort(permutation))])
ggplot(importance, aes(share, predictor, fill = method)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colours[1:2], guide = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Share of the total importance", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
Code 
rank_gain <- names(sort(gain, decreasing = TRUE)); rank_perm <- names(sort(permutation, decreasing = TRUE))

By gain the order is Age (days), Cement, Water; by permutation it is Age (days), Cement, Water. The top predictor, age (days), accounts for 37% of the permutation importance: shuffling it raises the test RMSE by 12.1 MPa. The two measures give the same order here, but they need not. Gain tends to favour predictors with many possible split points, and both measures share the credit unfairly between predictors that are correlated (here water and superplasticizer, for example). Importance says how much the model uses a predictor, not in which direction, and not whether changing it would change the strength.

Which way? Partial dependence

A partial dependence plot shows the average prediction as one predictor moves across its range. For each value \(v\), we set the predictor to \(v\) in every training sample, predict, and average:

\[\text{PD}(v) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{F}\left(v,\; x_{i,\text{other}}\right)\]

Code 
partial_dependence <- function(fit, x, feature, grid) {
  data.frame(value = grid,
             prediction = sapply(grid, function(v) { x[, feature] <- v; mean(predict(fit, x)) }))
}
top4 <- rank_perm[1:4]
pd <- do.call(rbind, lapply(top4, function(v) {
  grid <- seq(quantile(train[[v]], 0.01), quantile(train[[v]], 0.99), length.out = 40)
  cbind(feature = nice[[v]], partial_dependence(fit, x_train, v, grid))
}))
pd$feature <- factor(pd$feature, levels = nice[top4])
Code 
ggplot(pd, aes(value, prediction)) +
  geom_line(colour = colours[1], linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ feature, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Value of the predictor", y = "Average predicted strength (MPa)") +
  theme_bw()

These are the shapes the straight line could not draw. Strength rises quickly with age and then flattens; it rises with cement; it falls with water. Where a curve is flat, the model sees no further change. The curve is only a summary of the average: if the effect of a predictor depends on another (an interaction), the average hides it. A partial dependence for two predictors at once shows it. Here is the effect of slag, with the age set to 3 days, 28 days and one year for every sample:

Code 
slag_grid <- seq(0, quantile(train$slag, 0.99), length.out = 40)
pd_int <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(3, 28, 365), function(a) {
  x_age <- x_train; x_age[, "age"] <- a                 # every sample gets this age
  cbind(age = paste(a, "days"), partial_dependence(fit, x_age, "slag", slag_grid))
}))
pd_int$age <- factor(pd_int$age, levels = c("3 days", "28 days", "365 days"))
ggplot(pd_int, aes(value, prediction, colour = age)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = colours[1:3]) +
  labs(x = "Blast furnace slag (kg per m³)", y = "Average predicted strength (MPa)", colour = "Age") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
Code 
rise <- tapply(pd_int$prediction, pd_int$age, function(p) p[length(p)] - p[1])

The lines are far from parallel: going from no slag to 290 kg changes the predicted strength by 5.3 MPa at 3 days, 18.0 MPa at 28 days and 14.3 MPa at one year. The model has found the interaction of section 2 without being told.

One sample at a time: SHAP values

SHAP values (SHapley Additive exPlanations; Lundberg & Lee, 2017) split the prediction for one sample among the predictors, so that

\[\hat{F}(x) = \underbrace{\phi_0}_{\text{average prediction}} + \phi_{\text{cement}} + \phi_{\text{water}} + \dots + \phi_{\text{age}}\]

Each \(\phi_j\) is the contribution of predictor \(j\) for this sample: how many MPa it moves the prediction up or down from the average. For tree models they can be computed exactly and quickly, and xgboost does it with predict(..., predcontrib = TRUE):

Code 
shap <- predict(fit, x_test, predcontrib = TRUE)
colnames(shap)
[1] "cement"           "slag"             "fly_ash"          "water"            "superplasticizer" "coarse"           "fine"             "age"              "(Intercept)"
Code 
# the contributions and the (Intercept) column (the average prediction) add up to the prediction
all.equal(unname(rowSums(shap)), unname(predict(fit, x_test)), tolerance = 1e-4)
[1] TRUE

The last column, (Intercept), is \(\phi_0\). The check shows that for every test sample, the contributions add up to the prediction. Here are two samples: the one the model predicts to be strongest, and the one it predicts to be weakest:

Code 
pred_test <- unname(predict(fit, x_test))
two <- c(strong = which.max(pred_test), weak = which.min(pred_test))
shap_two <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(two), function(k) {
  i <- two[[k]]
  data.frame(sample = factor(k, levels = c("strong", "weak"),
                             labels = c(paste0("Strongest predicted: ", f1(pred_test[i]), " MPa"),
                                        paste0("Weakest predicted: ", f1(pred_test[i]), " MPa"))),
             label = paste0(nice[predictors], " = ", sapply(x_test[i, predictors], function(v) format(v, digits = 3))),
             shap = shap[i, predictors])
}))
shap_two$direction <- factor(ifelse(shap_two$shap > 0, "Raises", "Lowers"), levels = c("Raises", "Lowers"))
shap_two$label <- reorder(shap_two$label, abs(shap_two$shap))
ggplot(shap_two, aes(shap, label, fill = direction)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ sample, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colours[1:2]) +
  labs(x = "Contribution to the prediction (MPa)", y = NULL, fill = "Prediction") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
Code 
base <- shap[1, "(Intercept)"]

Start from the average prediction, 35.6 MPa. For the strongest sample, the bars to the right push the prediction up, to 74.9 MPa, and for the weakest the bars to the left pull it down to 5.0 MPa. The labels show the value of each predictor in that sample, so each bar can be read as a sentence (“with this much water, the prediction goes down by so many MPa”).

Averaging the size of the SHAP values over all test samples gives a global importance that, unlike gain, is based on what the model does for each sample. Plotting all of them shows the direction too:

Code 
shap_all <- as.data.frame(shap[, predictors])
mean_abs <- sort(colMeans(abs(shap_all)), decreasing = TRUE)
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(predictors, function(v)
  data.frame(feature = nice[[v]], shap = shap_all[[v]],
             value = factor(ifelse(test[[v]] > median(train[[v]]), "High", "Low"), levels = c("Low", "High")))))
long$feature <- factor(long$feature, levels = rev(nice[names(mean_abs)]))
set.seed(7)
ggplot(long, aes(shap, feature, colour = value)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = colours[1:2]) +
  labs(x = "SHAP value: contribution to the prediction (MPa)", y = NULL,
       colour = "Value of the predictor\n(against the training median)") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Each point is one test sample. High values of cement (orange) sit on the right: they push the strength up. High values of water sit on the left. For age, the picture is more mixed, because the effect of age is not a straight line: young concrete is pulled down by more MPa than old concrete is pushed up. Ordered by mean size, the top predictors are Age (days), Cement, Water.

8. Caveats

Tuning sensitivity. Boosting is more sensitive to its settings than a random forest. A learning rate that is too high, or too many deep trees, can overfit badly, as the charts above show. Always choose the number of trees by cross-validation or a validation set, never by what looks good on the training data, and never on the test set. The tuning grid here is small; with more computing time one would search more finely (random search, or Bayesian optimisation).

Extrapolation. A tree predicts an average of samples it has seen, so the prediction stays flat outside the range of the data. A boosted model cannot predict that concrete with more cement than any in the data will be even stronger; and the model knows nothing about concrete older than a year. A linear model would extrapolate (not necessarily well). Be careful with mixes unlike the training data.

Code 
g <- seq(300, 700, length.out = 60)
ext <- partial_dependence(fit, x_train, "cement", g)
ggplot(ext, aes(value, prediction)) +
  geom_line(colour = colours[1], linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = max(train$cement), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = max(train$cement), y = min(ext$prediction), label = "most cement in the data",
           hjust = 1.05, vjust = -0.5, colour = "grey20") +
  labs(x = "Cement (kg per m³)", y = "Average predicted strength (MPa)") +
  theme_bw()

Beyond the dashed line the prediction is a flat line: it is not a forecast, it is only what the model does at the edge of what it knows.

Importance is not causation. The predictors in these data are related to each other: engineers add superplasticizer in order to use less water, and mixes with slag are designed differently from those without. So a large importance or a steep partial dependence for water does not mean that adding water to a given concrete will lower its strength by that amount. The model shows what goes with strength in these data, which is what prediction needs. Causal questions need an experiment or a causal design.

Other things to keep in mind.

  • The data are one study, from one laboratory: the model describes these mixes and materials. Cement from other suppliers may behave differently.
  • The 25 duplicated rows may sit in both the training and the validation parts of a cross-validation fold, which makes the validation error a little too optimistic. The test set may share a few of them too.
  • The test result rests on 206 samples and one random split. Repeating the split, or using nested cross-validation, would give a more stable estimate.
  • Boosting predicts the average strength for a mix. It does not by itself give a prediction interval; for safety decisions you need one (for example from quantile loss, or conformal prediction).

9. Reporting the results in APA style

Report a predictive model as you would any other: what was predicted and from what, how the data were split, how the settings were chosen, and how well the model did on data it had not seen.

Method:

We predicted the compressive strength of concrete (MPa) from seven mix ingredients and age, using gradient boosting with squared-error loss (xgboost, version 3.2.1.1; Chen & Guestrin, 2016). The 1,030 samples (Yeh, 1998) were split at random into a training set (n = 824) and a test set (n = 206). The settings were chosen on the training set by five-fold cross-validation over a grid of 36 combinations of learning rate, tree depth, minimum child weight and row sampling; the number of trees was chosen by early stopping. The selected model had a learning rate of 0.1, a maximum depth of 4, a minimum child weight of 1, row sampling of 1, column sampling of 0.8 and 888 trees. We compared it on the test set with linear regression, a pruned regression tree and a random forest with default settings (ranger; Wright & Ziegler, 2017). Predictors were explained with gain, permutation importance, partial dependence and SHAP values (Lundberg & Lee, 2017).

Results:

On the test set, gradient boosting predicted concrete strength with an RMSE of 3.93 MPa, an MAE of 2.78 MPa and R² = .95. This was better than linear regression (RMSE = 10.43, R² = .61) and a single regression tree (RMSE = 9.60, R² = .67), and better than an untuned random forest (RMSE = 5.66, R² = .89). The most important predictors were age (days), cement, water (permutation importance), and the partial dependence plots showed that strength rose steeply with age at first and then levelled off.

Table 1

Test-Set Performance of Four Models Predicting the Compressive Strength of Concrete

RMSE MAE R2
Linear regression 10.43 8.41 0.61
Single tree 9.60 7.45 0.67
Random forest 5.66 4.43 0.89
Gradient boosting 3.93 2.78 0.95

Note. N = 206 test samples. RMSE = root mean squared error; MAE = mean absolute error (both in MPa); R² = 1 − SSE/SST on the test set.

Points to remember:

  • Say that the performance is measured on a test set (or by cross-validation) and never on the data used for fitting.
  • Report the error in the units of the outcome (RMSE, MAE), and \(R^2\) if it helps; compare with a simple baseline, not only with “nothing”.
  • Report all the settings, the number of trees and how they were chosen, and the package versions.
  • Set and report the random seed: boosting with row and column sampling is random.
  • Say what the importance and the partial dependence mean, and that they are not causal effects.
  • Cite R, the packages (citation("xgboost")) and the data.

10. Summary

When A continuous outcome, a table of numbers, curved effects and interactions you do not want to specify by hand
Idea Start from the mean; fit a small tree to the residuals; add it, scaled by a learning rate; repeat
Loss and gradient Squared error: the negative gradient is the residual. Other losses give other “residuals”
How (R) xgb.train(params, xgb.DMatrix(x, label = y), nrounds); xgb.cv() for cross-validation and early stopping
Main settings Learning rate, number of trees, depth, row and column sampling, minimum child weight, penalties
Overfitting Too many trees overfit: choose the number of trees by cross-validation with early stopping
Compare with A baseline model, and a random forest; judge on a test set with RMSE, MAE and \(R^2\)
Interpretation Gain and permutation importance; partial dependence; SHAP values with predict(..., predcontrib = TRUE)
Cautions Sensitive to tuning; flat outside the range of the data; importance is not causation

References

Breiman, L. (2001). Random forests. Machine Learning, 45(1), 5–32. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1010933404324

Chen, T., & Guestrin, C. (2016). XGBoost: A scalable tree boosting system. In Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (pp. 785–794). ACM. https://doi.org/10.1145/2939672.2939785

Chen, T., He, T., Benesty, M., Khotilovich, V., Tang, Y., Cho, H., Chen, K., Mitchell, R., Cano, I., Zhou, T., Li, M., Xie, J., Lin, M., Geng, Y., Li, Y., & Yuan, J. (2026). xgboost: Extreme gradient boosting (R package version 3.2.1.1). https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=xgboost

Friedman, J. H. (2001). Greedy function approximation: A gradient boosting machine. The Annals of Statistics, 29(5), 1189–1232. https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1013203451

Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R., & Friedman, J. (2009). The elements of statistical learning: Data mining, inference, and prediction (2nd ed.). Springer.

Lundberg, S. M., & Lee, S.-I. (2017). A unified approach to interpreting model predictions. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (Vol. 30, pp. 4765–4774).

Molnar, C. (2022). Interpretable machine learning: A guide for making black box models explainable (2nd ed.). https://christophm.github.io/interpretable-ml-book/

Therneau, T., & Atkinson, B. (2026). rpart: Recursive partitioning and regression trees (R package version 4.1.27). https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=rpart

Wright, M. N., & Ziegler, A. (2017). ranger: A fast implementation of random forests for high dimensional data in C++ and R. Journal of Statistical Software, 77(1), 1–17. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v077.i01

Yeh, I.-C. (1998). Modeling of strength of high-performance concrete using artificial neural networks. Cement and Concrete Research, 28(12), 1797–1808. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0008-8846(98)00165-3

Yeh, I.-C. (2007). Concrete compressive strength [Data set]. UCI Machine Learning Repository. https://doi.org/10.24432/C5PK67

This post first appeared on Worked Examples in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Ordinal Logistic Regression: What Makes People Satisfied With Their Job?
item.description: Ordinal logistic regression (the proportional odds model) in R with MASS::polr(), on the 2022 General Social Survey: how autonomy, respect, job security, stress and working from home go with the job satisfaction of about 2,200 US workers, with odds ratios, thresholds, predicted probabilities, the proportional odds assumption and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Ordinal logistic regression (the proportional odds model) in R with MASS::polr(), on the 2022 General Social Survey: how autonomy, respect, job security, stress and working from home go with the job satisfaction of about 2,200 US workers, with odds ratios, thresholds, predicted probabilities, the proportional odds assumption and APA reporting.

The question: four answers in order

Since 1972 the General Social Survey (GSS) has asked Americans: “On the whole, how satisfied are you with the work you do — would you say you are very satisfied, moderately satisfied, a little dissatisfied, or very dissatisfied?” In 2022 it also asked them about the job itself: are they free to decide how to do their work, are they treated with respect, is the job secure, how often is it stressful, how often do they work from home?

This page asks: which of these go with being more satisfied with one’s job? Does working from home make people happier with their work, or is it something else?

The answer has four values in order: very dissatisfied, a little dissatisfied, moderately satisfied, very satisfied. But nobody knows how far apart they are: the step from “a little dissatisfied” to “moderately satisfied” may be bigger than the step from “moderately” to “very”. The type of outcome decides the type of regression:

Outcome Regression Example
Two categories logistic hired or not
Ordered categories ordinal logistic job satisfaction: very dissatisfied … very satisfied
Unordered categories multinomial logistic how someone left a job: quit, retired, laid off…

Three other ways to analyse the answers, and what each gets wrong:

  • A linear regression on the scores 1 to 4 assumes the four answers are equally far apart, and predicts answers such as 3.4 that nobody can give.
  • A logistic regression of satisfied against dissatisfied throws away the difference between “moderately” and “very” satisfied, where most people are.
  • A multinomial logistic regression ignores the order, and needs a whole set of coefficients for every answer: 27 parameters here instead of 11.

The ordinal logistic regression uses the order and needs one coefficient per predictor.

Code 
library(MASS)      # polr(): ordinal logistic regression (comes with R)
library(ordinal)   # clm(), nominal_test(): checks the proportional odds assumption
library(haven)     # read_dta(): reads the Stata files of the GSS
library(ggplot2)
# one colour per answer, from red (dissatisfied) to blue (satisfied), the same in every chart
satisfaction <- c("Very dissatisfied", "A little dissatisfied", "Moderately satisfied", "Very satisfied")
colours <- setNames(c("#c23b3a", "#ec8a85", "#6da7ec", "#1c5cab"), satisfaction)
ink     <- setNames(c("white", "#0b0b0b", "#0b0b0b", "white"), satisfaction)  # labels on the bars
# number formats for the text
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^0", "", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))

1. The data

The GSS is run by NORC at the University of Chicago. Its data are free and need no login: one file per survey year. 2022 is the latest year with the Quality of Working Life module, a set of questions about work designed by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) and asked of everyone who had a job. The Stata file comes in a zip of 6 MB.

Code 
options(timeout = max(300, getOption("timeout")))   # allow slow downloads
zip <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")
download.file("https://gss.norc.org/content/dam/gss/get-the-data/documents/stata/2022_stata.zip",
              zip, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
dta <- unzip(zip, files = "2022/GSS2022.dta", exdir = tempdir())
# the questions we need, out of the 1,297 columns in the file
columns <- c("satjob", "wkfreedm", "respect", "jobsecok", "stress", "wrkhome", "wrkslf", "age", "mode")
raw <- read_dta(dta, col_select = tidyselect::all_of(columns))
nrow(raw)
[1] 4149

Each answer is stored as a number with a label. “Don’t know”, “no answer”, “skipped on the web” and “not asked” (people without a job are not asked about their job) are special missing codes, which read_dta() turns into NA:

Code 
attr(raw$satjob, "labels")[1:4]       # the four answers and their codes
       very satisfied  moderately satisfied a little dissatisfied     very dissatisfied 
                    1                     2                     3                     4
Code 
table(raw$satjob, useNA = "ifany")    # NA: not asked or not answered

   1    2    3    4 <NA> 
1268 1237  316  132 1196

The codes run from very satisfied (1) to very dissatisfied (4). We turn them round, so that a higher number always means more of something: more satisfied, more freedom, more often stressed. The predictors:

Predictor Question Answers, coded
autonomy I am given a lot of freedom to decide how to do my own work 1 not at all true, 2 not too true, 3 somewhat true, 4 very true
respect At the place where I work, I am treated with respect 1 strongly disagree, 2 disagree, 3 agree, 4 strongly agree
security The job security is good 1 not at all true … 4 very true
stress How often do you find your work stressful? 1 never, 2 hardly ever, 3 sometimes, 4 often, 5 always
home How often do you work at home as part of your job? never; some days (from a few times a year to more than once a week); mainly at home
self_employed Are you self-employed or do you work for someone else? no, yes
age10 Age in decades: 4.1 = 41 years
Code 
n <- function(x) as.numeric(x)   # drops the labels, keeps the NAs
d <- data.frame(
  satisfaction  = factor(5 - n(raw$satjob), levels = 1:4, labels = satisfaction, ordered = TRUE),
  autonomy      = 5 - n(raw$wkfreedm),
  respect       = 5 - n(raw$respect),
  security      = 5 - n(raw$jobsecok),
  stress        = 6 - n(raw$stress),
  home          = cut(n(raw$wrkhome), c(0, 1, 5, 6), labels = c("Never", "Some days", "Mainly")),
  self_employed = factor(ifelse(n(raw$wrkslf) == 1, "Yes", "No"), levels = c("No", "Yes")),
  age10         = n(raw$age) / 10,
  web           = factor(ifelse(n(raw$mode) == 4, "Yes", "No"), levels = c("No", "Yes")))  # answered on the web
vars <- c("satisfaction", "autonomy", "respect", "security", "stress", "home", "self_employed", "age10")
d <- d[complete.cases(d[vars]), ]
nrow(d)
[1] 2167

factor(..., ordered = TRUE) makes an ordered factor: R now knows that “very satisfied” is above “moderately satisfied”. polr() needs it. That leaves 2,167 people who answered all the questions.

The four questions with agree or true answers are treated as numbers: one coefficient for each step up the scale. This assumes every step has the same effect; section 7 checks it.

2. Look at the data

Code 
overall <- prop.table(table(d$satisfaction))
round(100 * overall, 1)

    Very dissatisfied A little dissatisfied  Moderately satisfied        Very satisfied 
                  3.5                   9.8                  42.2                  44.5

Most people are satisfied with their work: 45% very and 42% moderately. Only 3.5% are very dissatisfied, a typical skew for job satisfaction. How does satisfaction change with each predictor?

Code 
# the answers to each question, in words
answers <- list(autonomy = c("Not at all true", "Not too true", "Somewhat true", "Very true"),
                respect  = c("Strongly disagree", "Disagree", "Agree", "Strongly agree"),
                security = c("Not at all true", "Not too true", "Somewhat true", "Very true"),
                stress   = c("Never", "Hardly ever", "Sometimes", "Often", "Always"),
                home     = c("Never", "Some days", "Mainly"))
questions <- c(autonomy = "Autonomy", respect = "Respect", security = "Security",
               stress = "Stress", home = "From home")
# stacked bars of shares (each bar adds up to 100%), one panel per question, larger shares labelled
stacked <- function(m, x_label) {
  ggplot(m, aes(share, answer, fill = satisfaction)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.8, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
    geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(share >= 0.07, pct(share), ""), colour = satisfaction),
              position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
    facet_grid(question ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colours) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = ink, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) sub("^[^:]*: ", "", x)) +   # drop the question from the label
    labs(x = x_label, y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.margin = margin(5.5, 18, 5.5, 5.5)) +  # room for "100%"
    guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
}
# how satisfied the people who gave each answer are, with the number of people
observed <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(answers), function(v) {
  answer <- factor(answers[[v]][as.integer(d[[v]])], levels = answers[[v]])
  shares <- as.data.frame(prop.table(table(answer, satisfaction = d$satisfaction), 1), responseName = "share")
  size   <- table(answer)
  # "Autonomy: Very true (1,065)"; the question keeps the labels of different panels apart
  labels <- paste0(questions[[v]], ": ", names(size), " (", num(as.vector(size)), ")")
  shares$answer   <- factor(labels[as.integer(shares$answer)], levels = rev(labels))
  shares$question <- factor(questions[[v]], levels = questions)
  shares
}))
stacked(observed, "share of the people who gave this answer (number of people)")
Code 
share <- function(v) prop.table(table(d[[v]], d$satisfaction), 1)
by_respect  <- share("respect")
by_autonomy <- share("autonomy")
by_stress   <- share("stress")
by_home     <- share("home")
dissatisfied <- c("Very dissatisfied", "A little dissatisfied")
  • Respect: 63% of the people who strongly agree that they are treated with respect are very satisfied, against 13% of those who disagree. 41% of those who disagree are dissatisfied. The 48 people who strongly disagree do not follow the pattern; the group is small, and its shares are uncertain.
  • Autonomy and job security go the same way: the more of them, the more people are very satisfied.
  • Stress: 72% of the people whose work is never stressful are very satisfied, and 24% of those whose work is always stressful.
  • Working from home: 48% of the people who work from home on some days are very satisfied, against 42% of those who never do. A small difference, in favour of working from home.

But the predictors go together. People who can work from home also tend to be freer to decide how to do their work:

Code 
round(100 * prop.table(table(home = d$home, autonomy = d$autonomy), 1))   # % of each row
           autonomy
home         1  2  3  4
  Never      5 13 39 44
  Some days  2  9 35 55
  Mainly     3  5 35 57
Code 
free <- prop.table(table(d$home, d$autonomy), 1)[, "4"]

55% of the people who work from home on some days say “very true” to the freedom question, against 44% of those who never do. So is it working from home that goes with satisfaction, or the freedom? The model can tell: it estimates the effect of each predictor holding the others constant.

3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: cut the scale in three places

Four ordered answers can be split into “this answer or lower” against “higher” in three places:

Split \(j\) Lower: \(Y \le j\) Higher: \(Y > j\)
1 very dissatisfied a little dissatisfied or more
2 dissatisfied (very or a little) satisfied (moderately or very)
3 moderately satisfied or less very satisfied

\(P(Y_i \le j)\) is a cumulative probability: the probability that person \(i\) gives answer \(j\) or a lower one.

Step 2: one logistic regression per split, with the same slopes

\[\text{logit}\,P(Y_i \le j) = \ln\frac{P(Y_i \le j)}{P(Y_i > j)} = \theta_j - (\beta_1 x_{1i} + \dots + \beta_p x_{pi}), \qquad j = 1, 2, 3\]

Each split has its own intercept, \(\theta_j\), called a threshold or cut-point. The slopes \(\beta\) are the same at all three splits: a predictor changes the odds of a higher answer by the same factor wherever the scale is cut. This is the proportional odds assumption, and the model is also called the proportional odds model.

The thresholds increase, \(\theta_1 < \theta_2 < \theta_3\), because \(P(Y \le j)\) can only grow with \(j\). The minus sign makes a positive \(\beta\) mean higher answers: here, more satisfied. R’s polr() and clm() and SPSS’s PLUM write the model this way; some programs, for example SAS, write it with a plus sign, and their coefficients have the opposite sign.

Step 3: from the splits to the four answers

Write \(\eta_i = \beta_1 x_{1i} + \dots + \beta_p x_{pi}\). Then

\[P(Y_i \le j) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\theta_j - \eta_i)}}\]

and the probability of each answer is the difference between two cumulative probabilities:

\[P(Y_i = 1) = P(Y_i \le 1) \qquad P(Y_i = j) = P(Y_i \le j) - P(Y_i \le j - 1) \qquad P(Y_i = 4) = 1 - P(Y_i \le 3)\]

The four probabilities are between 0 and 1 and add up to 1.

Step 4: what a coefficient means

\(e^{\beta}\) is a cumulative odds ratio: the number by which the odds of a higher answer rather than a lower one are multiplied for each step up the predictor, with the other predictors held constant. With proportional odds the same number holds at every split. An odds ratio of 2 for respect means that one step up the respect scale doubles the odds of being very satisfied rather than less satisfied, and doubles the odds of being satisfied rather than dissatisfied, and doubles the odds of being anything but very dissatisfied.

Step 5: the picture behind the model, a hidden satisfaction scale

Imagine that each person has a hidden, continuous satisfaction, \(Y^*\), which depends on the predictors plus a random part:

\[Y^*_i = \eta_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \text{logistic}(0, 1)\]

The person answers by where \(Y^*\) falls among the thresholds: “very dissatisfied” below \(\theta_1\), “a little dissatisfied” between \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\), “moderately satisfied” between \(\theta_2\) and \(\theta_3\), “very satisfied” above \(\theta_3\). The predictors move the whole distribution of \(Y^*\) to the right or to the left; the thresholds stay where they are. This gives exactly the formulas of steps 2 and 3. With a normal \(\varepsilon\) instead of a logistic one, it is the ordinal probit model (polr(..., method = "probit")). Section 5 draws the picture with the fitted numbers.

Step 6: how R finds the numbers

By maximum likelihood: R looks for the thresholds and the \(\beta\)’s that make the answers people actually gave as probable as possible,

\[\ln L = \sum_i \ln P(Y_i = \text{the answer that person } i \text{ gave})\]

Step 7: count the parameters

Three thresholds, plus one slope for each of autonomy, respect, security, stress, self-employment and age, plus two for working from home (three groups): 11 parameters. A multinomial model with the same predictors needs 9 coefficients for each of the three answers other than the reference: 27.

4. Fitting the model

Code 
fit <- polr(satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + self_employed + age10,
            data = d, Hess = TRUE)
summary(fit)
Call:
polr(formula = satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + security + 
    stress + home + self_employed + age10, data = d, Hess = TRUE)
Coefficients:
                    Value Std. Error t value
autonomy          0.39481    0.06005   6.574
respect           0.72743    0.07253  10.030
security          0.38234    0.05863   6.521
stress           -0.37740    0.04807  -7.852
homeSome days     0.15549    0.10266   1.515
homeMainly       -0.07595    0.12017  -0.632
self_employedYes  0.45185    0.14198   3.182
age10             0.15250    0.03194   4.775
Intercepts:
                                           Value   Std. Error t value
Very dissatisfied|A little dissatisfied     0.6519  0.3782     1.7239
A little dissatisfied|Moderately satisfied  2.3162  0.3722     6.2236
Moderately satisfied|Very satisfied         4.8746  0.3856    12.6427
Residual Deviance: 4065.195 
AIC: 4087.195

Hess = TRUE keeps the matrix that summary() needs for the standard errors; without it, summary() fits the model again.

How to read the output

Code 
b     <- coef(fit)                          # the slopes
theta <- fit$zeta                           # the thresholds
se    <- sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))[names(b)]
z     <- b / se
p     <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))                 # summary() prints no p values: compute them
or    <- exp(b)                             # odds ratios
ci    <- exp(confint(fit))                  # their 95% confidence intervals (profile likelihood)
Part Meaning Here
Coefficients One slope \(\beta\) per predictor term, with its standard error and \(t = \beta / SE\). Positive: more satisfied respect: \(\beta\) = 0.73, SE = 0.07
Intercepts The thresholds \(\theta_j\), named after the two answers they separate Moderately satisfied|Very satisfied: 4.87
Residual Deviance \(-2 \ln L\): how badly the model fits; smaller is better. Used for the tests in section 6 4,065
AIC The deviance plus 2 for every parameter, for comparing models fitted to the same data 4,087
  • There are no p values. The t value is really a \(z\): compare it with the normal distribution. For respect, z = 10.03, p < .001.
  • The thresholds are the cut-points on the hidden scale for someone with every predictor at 0. Here that person does not exist (autonomy and respect start at 1, age at 18), so the thresholds mean little on their own; they are needed for the predicted probabilities.
  • One coefficient per predictor, not one per answer: that is the gain over the multinomial model.

The odds ratios:

Code 
terms <- c(autonomy = "Autonomy (per step)", respect = "Respect (per step)",
           security = "Job security (per step)", stress = "Stress (per step)",
           "homeSome days" = "Works from home some days (vs never)",
           homeMainly = "Works mainly from home (vs never)",
           self_employedYes = "Self-employed (vs employee)", age10 = "Age (per 10 years)")
or_table <- data.frame(Predictor    = terms,
                       `Odds ratio` = f2(or[names(terms)]),
                       `95% CI`     = paste0("[", f2(ci[names(terms), 1]), ", ", f2(ci[names(terms), 2]), "]"),
                       p            = sapply(p[names(terms)], function(x) sub("= ", "", pval(x))),
                       check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
knitr::kable(or_table, align = "lrrr")
Predictor Odds ratio 95% CI p
Autonomy (per step) 1.48 [1.32, 1.67] < .001
Respect (per step) 2.07 [1.80, 2.39] < .001
Job security (per step) 1.47 [1.31, 1.64] < .001
Stress (per step) 0.69 [0.62, 0.75] < .001
Works from home some days (vs never) 1.17 [0.96, 1.43] .130
Works mainly from home (vs never) 0.93 [0.73, 1.17] .527
Self-employed (vs employee) 1.57 [1.19, 2.08] .001
Age (per 10 years) 1.16 [1.09, 1.24] < .001

All at the same values of the other predictors:

  • Respect matters most: each step up the scale, for example from “agree” to “strongly agree”, multiplies the odds of a higher satisfaction answer by 2.07.
  • Autonomy (1.48 per step) and job security (1.47) also go with more satisfaction.
  • Stress goes the other way: each step more often stressful cuts the odds of a higher answer by 31% (odds ratio 0.69).
  • The self-employed have 1.57 times the odds of employees of a higher answer, and the odds rise by 16% with every 10 years of age.
  • Working from home: the confidence intervals include 1. Once autonomy, respect, security and stress are held constant, there is no clear difference between those who work from home and those who never do.

Working from home alone does go with more satisfaction, as section 2 showed:

Code 
home_alone <- polr(satisfaction ~ home, data = d)
round(exp(coef(home_alone)), 2)
homeSome days    homeMainly 
         1.38          1.25

On its own, working from home some days has an odds ratio of 1.38; with the other predictors, 1.17. The jobs that can be done from home also give more freedom and security, and these, not the place of work, carry the difference.

The same numbers by hand

Steps 2 and 3 for a typical worker: the median answer to each question, the median age, never works from home, an employee.

Code 
sapply(d[c("autonomy", "respect", "security", "stress", "age10")], median)   # the medians
autonomy  respect security   stress    age10 
     3.0      3.0      4.0      3.0      4.1
Code 
x    <- c(autonomy = 3, respect = 3, security = 4, stress = 3,
          "homeSome days" = 0, homeMainly = 0, self_employedYes = 0, age10 = 4.1)
eta  <- sum(b * x[names(b)])                      # the place on the hidden scale
cum  <- plogis(theta - eta)                       # step 3: P(Y <= j), j = 1, 2, 3
prob <- setNames(diff(c(0, cum, 1)), satisfaction)  # P(Y = j)
round(prob, 3)
    Very dissatisfied A little dissatisfied  Moderately satisfied        Very satisfied 
                0.023                 0.088                 0.507                 0.381
Code 
# new people for predict(), with the factor levels of the model
people <- function(...) {
  x <- data.frame(...)
  for (v in intersect(names(x), c("home", "self_employed"))) x[[v]] <- factor(x[[v]], levels = levels(d[[v]]))
  x
}
typical <- people(autonomy = 3, respect = 3, security = 4, stress = 3, home = "Never",
                  self_employed = "No", age10 = 4.1)
round(predict(fit, newdata = typical, type = "probs"), 3)   # the same, from R
    Very dissatisfied A little dissatisfied  Moderately satisfied        Very satisfied 
                0.023                 0.088                 0.507                 0.381

The typical worker is moderately satisfied with probability 51% and very satisfied with probability 38%.

5. Predicted probabilities: the easiest way to read the model

The hidden scale

Step 5 of section 3, with the fitted numbers: the hidden satisfaction of the typical worker if they disagree, and if they strongly agree, that they are treated with respect. Everything else stays the same.

Code 
two <- people(autonomy = 3, respect = c(2, 4), security = 4, stress = 3, home = "Never",
              self_employed = "No", age10 = 4.1)
person <- c("Disagrees that they are treated with respect", "Strongly agrees that they are treated with respect")
centre <- eta + b[["respect"]] * (c(2, 4) - 3)        # eta of each: the typical worker has respect = 3
probs2 <- predict(fit, newdata = two, type = "probs")
grid   <- seq(-2.5, 11, by = 0.01)
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(k)
  data.frame(person = person[k], y = grid, density = dlogis(grid, centre[k]),
             answer = cut(grid, c(-Inf, theta, Inf), labels = satisfaction))))
curves$person <- factor(curves$person, levels = person)
# the probability of each answer, printed above its part of the scale
middle <- c(theta[1] - 0.9, (theta[1] + theta[2]) / 2, (theta[2] + theta[3]) / 2, theta[3] + 1.6)
labels <- data.frame(person = factor(rep(person, each = 4), levels = person),
                     y = rep(middle, 2), share = as.vector(t(probs2)))
ggplot(curves, aes(y, density)) +
  geom_area(aes(fill = answer, group = answer), position = "identity") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey20") +
  # the thresholds stop below their names, the centre at the top of the curve
  geom_segment(data = data.frame(x = theta), aes(x = x, xend = x, y = 0, yend = 0.31),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_segment(data = data.frame(person = factor(person, levels = person), x = centre),
               aes(x = x, xend = x, y = 0, yend = dlogis(0)), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "grey20") +
  geom_text(data = labels, aes(y, 0.29, label = pct(share)), size = 3.2, colour = "grey15") +
  geom_text(data = data.frame(person = factor(rep(person, each = 3), levels = person), y = rep(theta, 2),
                              label = rep(paste0("theta[", 1:3, "]"), 2)),
            aes(y, 0.33, label = label), parse = TRUE, size = 3.4, colour = "grey30") +
  facet_wrap(~ person, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colours) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.345), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(title = "Where the hidden satisfaction of the typical worker falls",
       subtitle = "Dashed lines: the thresholds. Solid line: the centre of the distribution, eta.\nThe percentages are the areas: the probability of each answer.",
       x = "hidden satisfaction (Y*)", y = "density", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))

Strongly agreeing instead of disagreeing moves the centre of the distribution by \(2\beta\) = 1.45 to the right. The thresholds stay where they are, so more of the area falls above \(\theta_3\): the probability of “very satisfied” goes from 23% to 56%.

Predicted probabilities, one predictor at a time

The typical worker again, changing one predictor at a time:

Code 
vary <- function(v, values) {
  x <- typical[rep(1, length(values)), ]
  x[[v]] <- values
  pr <- predict(fit, newdata = x, type = "probs")
  labels <- paste0(questions[[v]], ": ", answers[[v]][values])
  data.frame(question = factor(questions[[v]], levels = questions),
             answer = factor(rep(labels, 4), levels = rev(labels)),
             satisfaction = factor(rep(satisfaction, each = length(values)), levels = satisfaction),
             share = as.vector(pr))
}
predicted <- rbind(vary("respect", 1:4), vary("autonomy", 1:4), vary("stress", 1:5))
predicted$question <- droplevels(predicted$question)
stacked(predicted, "predicted probability of each answer, for the typical worker")
Code 
p_resp   <- predict(fit, newdata = transform(typical[rep(1, 4), ], respect = 1:4), type = "probs")
p_stress <- predict(fit, newdata = transform(typical[rep(1, 5), ], stress = 1:5), type = "probs")
  • From “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree” that they are treated with respect, the probability that the typical worker is very satisfied rises from 13% to 56%, and the probability of being dissatisfied (very or a little) falls from 35% to 6%.
  • From work that is never stressful to work that is always stressful, “very satisfied” falls from 57% to 22%.
  • The odds ratio is the same at every step, the change in probability is not. Each step up the respect scale multiplies the odds by 2.07, but moves the probability of “very satisfied” by 10, 15, 18 percentage points: the effect on a probability depends on where a person starts.

Unlike the observed shares of section 2, these predictions follow the pattern of the model: every step up the respect scale helps, including the step from “strongly disagree” to “disagree”, which the few people who strongly disagree did not show.

6. Testing the predictors and the model

The likelihood-ratio test compares the deviances of two nested models. First the whole model against a model with thresholds only, then each predictor: drop it and see how much worse the model gets.

Code 
null <- polr(satisfaction ~ 1, data = d)
model_test <- anova(null, fit)
model_test
Likelihood ratio tests of ordinal regression models
Response: satisfaction
                                                                  Model Resid. df Resid. Dev   Test    Df LR stat. Pr(Chi)
1                                                                     1      2164   4632.148                              
2 autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + self_employed + age10      2156   4065.195 1 vs 2     8 566.9527       0
Code 
tests <- drop1(fit, test = "Chisq")
tests
Single term deletions
Model:
satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + 
    self_employed + age10
              Df    AIC     LRT  Pr(>Chi)    
<none>           4087.2                      
autonomy       1 4128.6  43.387 4.491e-11 ***
respect        1 4188.0 102.836 < 2.2e-16 ***
security       1 4127.8  42.591 6.748e-11 ***
stress         1 4148.2  62.972 2.096e-15 ***
home           2 4086.9   3.657  0.160641    
self_employed  1 4095.6  10.395  0.001264 ** 
age10          1 4108.2  23.048 1.580e-06 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
Code 
mcfadden <- 1 - deviance(fit) / deviance(null)   # McFadden's pseudo-R squared
mcfadden
[1] 0.1223952
  • Every predictor except working from home is significant. The \(\chi^2\) values rank them: respect (102.84), stress (62.97), autonomy (43.39) and job security (42.59), then age and self-employment. Working from home: \(\chi^2\)(2) = 3.66, p = .161.
  • McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\) = 0.12: one minus the deviance of the model divided by the deviance of the model with thresholds only. It runs much lower than the \(R^2\) of a linear regression; use it to compare models fitted to the same data.

Is the order worth using? The same predictors in a multinomial model, which ignores the order:

Code 
multi <- nnet::multinom(formula(fit), data = d, trace = FALSE)
data.frame(model      = c("ordinal (polr)", "multinomial (multinom)"),
           parameters = c(length(b) + length(theta), length(coef(multi))),
           AIC        = round(c(AIC(fit), AIC(multi)), 1))
                   model parameters    AIC
1         ordinal (polr)         11 4087.2
2 multinomial (multinom)         27 4115.9

The ordinal model fits better by AIC, with 11 parameters instead of 27: the multinomial model spends 16 more parameters and gains less than they cost.

How often does the model pick the right answer, if it picks the most likely one for each person?

Code 
guess <- predict(fit, type = "class")
table(observed = d$satisfaction, predicted = guess)
                       predicted
observed                Very dissatisfied A little dissatisfied Moderately satisfied Very satisfied
  Very dissatisfied                     6                    12                   48              9
  A little dissatisfied                 4                    10                  165             34
  Moderately satisfied                  1                    16                  574            323
  Very satisfied                        1                     8                  289            667
Code 
accuracy  <- mean(as.character(guess) == as.character(d$satisfaction))
base_rate <- max(overall)   # always guessing the most common answer
c(model = accuracy, most_common_answer = base_rate)
             model most_common_answer 
         0.5800646          0.4453161

58% right, against 45% for always guessing the most common answer. The model almost never predicts the two dissatisfied answers: they are rare, so for almost nobody are they the most likely answer. As in the multinomial example, the predicted probabilities carry the information, not the single best guess.

7. The proportional odds assumption

The model gives each predictor one slope for all three splits. Does it need three? A visual check first: fit a separate logistic regression at each split and compare the slopes.

Code 
splits <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(j) {
  dj <- transform(d, higher = as.integer(satisfaction) > j)   # TRUE above split j
  m  <- glm(update(formula(fit), higher ~ .), family = binomial, data = dj)
  data.frame(split = j, term = names(coef(m))[-1], b = coef(m)[-1], se = sqrt(diag(vcov(m)))[-1])
}))
short <- c(autonomy = "Autonomy", respect = "Respect", security = "Job security", stress = "Stress",
           "homeSome days" = "Home: some days", homeMainly = "Home: mainly",
           self_employedYes = "Self-employed", age10 = "Age (10 years)")
splits$term <- factor(short[splits$term], levels = short)
common      <- data.frame(term = factor(short, levels = short), b = b[names(short)])
ggplot(splits, aes(split, b)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey75") +
  geom_hline(data = common, aes(yintercept = b), colour = "#1c5cab", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = b - 1.96 * se, ymax = b + 1.96 * se), width = 0.15, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, colour = "grey15") +
  facet_wrap(~ term, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:3, limits = c(0.6, 3.4)) +
  labs(title = "The slope of each predictor at each split",
       subtitle = "Points: the slope from a separate logistic regression, with its 95% CI.\nDashed line: the one slope of the ordinal model.\nSplits: 1 very dissatisfied | the rest, 2 dissatisfied | satisfied, 3 very satisfied | the rest",
       x = "split", y = "slope (log odds of a higher answer)") +
  theme_bw()
Code 
security_splits <- splits$b[splits$term == short[["security"]]]

If the proportional odds assumption holds, the three points of each panel scatter around the dashed line, within their error bars. Most do. The clearest exception is job security: its slope grows from 0.07 at the first split to 0.45 at the third. Good job security seems to separate the very satisfied from the moderately satisfied more than it protects against being very dissatisfied. The confidence intervals are wide at the first split, though: only 75 people are very dissatisfied.

The formal test: fit the same model with clm() from the package ordinal, which can relax the assumption one predictor at a time. nominal_test() does that for each predictor and compares the two models with a likelihood-ratio test:

Code 
# the same model as polr(), with the same estimates
clm_fit <- clm(satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + self_employed + age10, data = d)
nominal <- nominal_test(clm_fit)
nominal
Tests of nominal effects
formula: satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + self_employed + age10
              Df  logLik    AIC    LRT Pr(>Chi)
<none>           -2032.6 4087.2                
autonomy       2 -2032.5 4091.0 0.1898   0.9095
respect        2 -2031.5 4088.9 2.2979   0.3170
security       2 -2030.8 4087.6 3.5963   0.1656
stress         2 -2032.3 4090.7 0.4917   0.7821
home           4 -2031.4 4092.9 2.3305   0.6752
self_employed  2 -2032.5 4090.9 0.2827   0.8682
age10          2 -2032.2 4090.4 0.7607   0.6836

No predictor needs its own slopes: the smallest p is .166, for job security. The differences that the chart shows could be chance. The Brant test (Brant, 1990), in the package brant, is a common alternative that answers the same question.

If the assumption fails: a partial proportional odds model

If a predictor did fail the test, it could get one slope per split while the others keep one slope: a partial proportional odds model (Peterson & Harrell, 1990). In clm(), the predictors in nominal get their own slopes:

Code 
partial <- clm(satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + stress + home + self_employed + age10,
               nominal = ~ security, data = d)
coef(partial)[grep("security", names(coef(partial)))]
   Very dissatisfied|A little dissatisfied.security A little dissatisfied|Moderately satisfied.security        Moderately satisfied|Very satisfied.security 
                                         -0.1968220                                          -0.3232832                                          -0.4471662
Code 
anova(clm_fit, partial)
Likelihood ratio tests of cumulative link models:
        formula:                                                                             nominal:  link: threshold:
clm_fit satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + security + stress + home + self_employed + age10 ~1        logit flexible  
partial satisfaction ~ autonomy + respect + stress + home + self_employed + age10            ~security logit flexible  
        no.par    AIC  logLik LR.stat df Pr(>Chisq)
clm_fit     11 4087.2 -2032.6                      
partial     13 4087.6 -2030.8  3.5963  2     0.1656

clm() writes these slopes as shifts of the thresholds, so the effect of security on a higher answer is the number shown with its sign changed: 0.20, 0.32, 0.45 at the three splits. The likelihood-ratio test is the same as the security row of nominal_test(), and the AIC is a little worse: two more parameters that do not pay for themselves. We keep the simple model. If several predictors failed, the alternatives are a model with every slope free (nominal = ~ ., the generalized ordered logit) or the multinomial model.

Four more things to keep in mind

Code 
# answers given as categories instead of numbers: one coefficient per answer
fit_steps <- update(fit, . ~ . - autonomy - respect - security - stress +
                      factor(autonomy) + factor(respect) + factor(security) + factor(stress))
steps_test <- anova(fit, fit_steps)
stress_steps <- coef(fit_steps)[paste0("factor(stress)", 2:5)]   # hardly ever ... always, against never
# the people who answered on the web against those interviewed in person or by phone
very_by_mode <- prop.table(table(d$web, d$satisfaction), 1)[, "Very satisfied"]
fit_mode <- update(fit, . ~ . + web)
round(cbind(without_mode = coef(fit), with_mode = coef(fit_mode)[names(coef(fit))]), 2)
                 without_mode with_mode
autonomy                 0.39      0.39
respect                  0.73      0.73
security                 0.38      0.37
stress                  -0.38     -0.37
homeSome days            0.16      0.17
homeMainly              -0.08     -0.06
self_employedYes         0.45      0.44
age10                    0.15      0.15
  • Equal steps. The four scored questions count each step up the scale the same. Treating the answers as categories instead, with a coefficient for each answer, fits somewhat better, \(\chi^2\)(9) = 21.73, p = .010: the steps are not all equal. For stress, for example, the coefficients of “hardly ever”, “sometimes”, “often” and “always” against “never” are -0.64, -0.83, -1.41, -1.59, not evenly spaced. The scored model is easier to read and tells the same story.
  • Web or interview. In 2022 most people answered the GSS on the web. 41% of them said “very satisfied”, against 49% of those interviewed in person or by phone, as people often give more positive answers when an interviewer is listening. Adding the mode to the model leaves the other coefficients almost unchanged (above).
  • The sample, not the population. These are unweighted estimates for the people in the survey. To describe all US workers, use the GSS weights (wtssps) and the design of the survey, for example with svyolr() in the package survey (Lumley, 2010).
  • Association, not cause. People who like their work may also see their workplace in a better light, and judge it more respectful and more secure. One survey at one point in time cannot tell which comes first.

8. Reporting the results in APA style

A report (APA 7th edition) needs the outcome and its order, the predictors and how they were scored, the model test, the check of the proportional odds assumption and the odds ratios with their uncertainty. The numbers come from the R objects, so the text below always matches the results:

Code 
n_model <- nrow(d)
lr      <- model_test$"LR stat."[2]
lr_df   <- model_test$"   Df"[2]
lr_p    <- model_test$"Pr(Chi)"[2]
ci_text <- function(t) paste0("95% CI [", f2(ci[t, 1]), ", ", f2(ci[t, 2]), "]")

Method (data analysis):

We analysed the 2,167 employed respondents to the 2022 General Social Survey (Davern et al., 2024) who answered the job satisfaction question and the Quality of Working Life questions used here. Job satisfaction (very dissatisfied, a little dissatisfied, moderately satisfied, very satisfied) was analysed with an ordinal logistic regression (proportional odds model). The predictors were autonomy, respect at work and job security (each scored 1–4) and work stress (scored 1–5), with higher scores meaning more; how often the respondent worked from home (never, some days, mainly); self-employment; and age. The proportional odds assumption was checked with likelihood-ratio tests of nominal effects. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the MASS (Venables & Ripley, 2002) and ordinal (Christensen, 2026) packages.

Results:

The predictors improved the fit over a thresholds-only model, χ²(8) = 566.95, p < .001, McFadden’s R² = .12, and no predictor departed from the proportional odds assumption (smallest p = .166). Holding the other predictors constant, respondents who felt more respected at work were more satisfied with their job, OR = 2.07, 95% CI [1.80, 2.39], as were those with more autonomy, OR = 1.48, 95% CI [1.32, 1.67], and better job security, OR = 1.47, 95% CI [1.31, 1.64]. More frequent stress went with lower satisfaction, OR = 0.69, 95% CI [0.62, 0.75]. Self-employed and older respondents were more satisfied (Table 1). How often respondents worked from home was not related to job satisfaction once the other predictors were held constant, χ²(2) = 3.66, p = .161.

Table 1

Odds Ratios From an Ordinal Logistic Regression of Job Satisfaction, General Social Survey 2022

Predictor Odds ratio 95% CI p
Autonomy (per step) 1.48 [1.32, 1.67] < .001
Respect (per step) 2.07 [1.80, 2.39] < .001
Job security (per step) 1.47 [1.31, 1.64] < .001
Stress (per step) 0.69 [0.62, 0.75] < .001
Works from home some days (vs never) 1.17 [0.96, 1.43] .130
Works mainly from home (vs never) 0.93 [0.73, 1.17] .527
Self-employed (vs employee) 1.57 [1.19, 2.08] .001
Age (per 10 years) 1.16 [1.09, 1.24] < .001

Note. N = 2,167. Odds ratios above 1 mean higher job satisfaction. Autonomy, respect and job security were scored 1–4 and stress 1–5, higher scores meaning more; age is in decades. Confidence intervals are profile-likelihood intervals.

Points to remember:

  • Say which way the outcome runs, and whether an odds ratio above 1 means a higher or a lower answer: programs differ.
  • Report odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and say that they hold the other predictors constant.
  • Give the model test (\(\chi^2\) with its degrees of freedom) and a pseudo-\(R^2\), and say which one.
  • Report the check of the proportional odds assumption, and what you did if it failed.
  • Predicted probabilities for typical people are easier to understand than odds ratios; show them where they help.
  • Cite R and the packages; citation("MASS") and citation("ordinal") give the references.

9. Summary

When The outcome is a category with three or more values in a natural order
Why not linear regression It assumes equal steps between the answers and predicts values nobody can give
Why not multinomial logistic regression It ignores the order and needs a set of coefficients for every answer
How (R) MASS::polr(y ~ x, data, Hess = TRUE), with y an ordered factor; or ordinal::clm()
Output Thresholds (one per split) and one slope per predictor; exp() of a slope is a cumulative odds ratio
Easiest to read Predicted probabilities: predict(fit, newdata, type = "probs")
Tests Likelihood-ratio tests with anova() and drop1(); McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\)
Assumptions Independent observations; proportional odds (the same slopes at every split)
If proportional odds fails A partial proportional odds model, clm(..., nominal = ~ x); or a multinomial model

References

Agresti, A. (2010). Analysis of ordinal categorical data (2nd ed.). Wiley.

Brant, R. (1990). Assessing proportionality in the proportional odds model for ordinal logistic regression. Biometrics, 46(4), 1171–1178. https://doi.org/10.2307/2532457

Christensen, R. H. B. (2026). ordinal: Regression models for ordinal data (R package version 2026.7-26). https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=ordinal

Davern, M., Bautista, R., Freese, J., Herd, P., & Morgan, S. L. (2024). General Social Survey 1972–2022 (Release 4) [Data set]. NORC at the University of Chicago. https://gss.norc.org/

Lumley, T. (2010). Complex surveys: A guide to analysis using R. Wiley.

McCullagh, P. (1980). Regression models for ordinal data. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological), 42(2), 109–142.

Peterson, B., & Harrell, F. E., Jr. (1990). Partial proportional odds models for ordinal response variables. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series C (Applied Statistics), 39(2), 205–217.

Venables, W. N., & Ripley, B. D. (2002). Modern applied statistics with S (4th ed.). Springer.

Wickham, H., Miller, E., & Smith, D. (2025). haven: Import and export ‘SPSS’, ‘Stata’ and ‘SAS’ files (R package version 2.5.5). https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.haven

This post first appeared on Worked Examples in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: How Did Federal Employees Leave in 2025?
item.description: Multinomial logistic regression in R with nnet::multinom(), on real OPM data: how about 330,000 US federal employees left their jobs in fiscal year 2025 (quit, retired, early retirement, deferred resignation, laid off, terminated), with relative risk ratios, predicted probabilities, the IIA assumption and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Multinomial logistic regression in R with nnet::multinom(), on real OPM data: how about 330,000 US federal employees left their jobs in fiscal year 2025 (quit, retired, early retirement, deferred resignation, laid off, terminated), with relative risk ratios, predicted probabilities, the IIA assumption and APA reporting.

The question: six ways to leave

In 2025 the US federal government lost staff in several ways at once. In January, most federal employees were offered a deferred resignation: stop working, stay on the payroll until 30 September 2025, then resign. Agencies offered early retirement, carried out reductions in force (layoffs) and dismissed staff. And people kept quitting and retiring, as they do every year.

So everyone who left federal service in 2025 left in one of six ways. This page asks: among the people who left, what made one way of leaving more likely than another? Did the young quit and the old retire? Who took the deferred resignation? Who was laid off?

The outcome is a category with six values and no natural order: quitting is not “more” or “less” than being laid off. The type of outcome decides the type of regression:

Outcome Regression Example
Two categories logistic hired or not
Ordered categories ordinal logistic a performance rating from 1 to 5
Unordered categories multinomial logistic how someone left: quit, retired, laid off…

A multinomial logistic regression picks one category as the reference and fits a logistic regression of each of the other categories against it, all at the same time. The data are real: the US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) publishes a record for every federal employee who leaves.

Code 
library(nnet)         # multinom(): multinomial logistic regression (comes with R)
library(nanoparquet)  # read_parquet(): reads the Parquet files that OPM publishes
library(ggplot2)
# one colour per way of leaving, the same in every chart
exits   <- c("Quit", "Retired", "Early retirement", "Deferred resignation", "Laid off", "Terminated")
colours <- setNames(c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100", "#e87ba4", "#008300"), exits)
ink     <- setNames(c("white", "white", "white", "#0b0b0b", "white", "white"), exits)  # labels on the bars
# number formats for the text
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^0", "", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num  <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
rr   <- function(x) ifelse(x >= 100, formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ","),
                           formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2))                   # relative risk ratios

1. The data

OPM’s Federal Workforce Data has a file for every month with one row per separation: a civilian employee leaving federal service. Each row says how the person left, their age group, years of service, agency, occupation, type of appointment and more. The files are free, need no login, and come through an API as Parquet files of one to four MB.

A monthly file holds the separations processed in that month, and some of them took effect months earlier: separations of September 2025 were still arriving in 2026. So we download every file from October 2023 to the latest one, and sort the separations by the date they took effect.

Code 
options(timeout = max(300, getOption("timeout")))   # allow slow downloads
# the list of monthly files, with the current version of each
files <- jsonlite::fromJSON("https://data.opm.gov/api/v1/files/separations?current=true")
files <- files[as.integer(files$year) * 100 + as.integer(files$month) >= 202310, ]
latest <- max(as.Date(paste(files$year, files$month, "01", sep = "-")))
# the columns we need, out of the 69 in each file
columns <- c("personnel_action_effective_date_yyyymm", "separation_category", "drp_indicator",
             "age_bracket", "length_of_service_years", "supervisory_status",
             "appointment_type", "stem_occupation")
# one month: download the file and read the columns; try again if OPM asks us to slow down
read_month <- function(year, month, version) {
  url  <- sprintf("https://data.opm.gov/api/v1/files/separations/%s/%s/%s/download", year, month, version)
  path <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
  for (attempt in 1:3) {
    ok <- tryCatch(download.file(url, path, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE) == 0, error = function(e) FALSE)
    if (ok) break
    Sys.sleep(10 * attempt)
  }
  if (!ok) stop("Could not download ", url)
  as.data.frame(read_parquet(path, col_select = columns))
}
raw <- do.call(rbind, Map(read_month, files$year, files$month, files$version))
nrow(raw)
[1] 808769

That is 36 monthly files, up to September 2026. The US federal fiscal year runs from October to September: fiscal year 2025 (FY2025) is October 2024 to September 2025. We keep FY2024, a year before the changes, and FY2025:

raw$fiscal_year <- ym %/% 100 + (ym %% 100 >= 10)              # October 2024 to September 2025 = 2025
